## Getting started

### What you will learn

This tutorial assumes **no previous R experience**. By the end you will be able to:

- read a spreadsheet (CSV file) into R and spot the problems in an untidy lab sheet;
- run quality-control checks that catch typing errors before any analysis;
- make publication-quality figures with **ggplot2**;
- describe growth, body proportions and allometry (how body regions scale with size), and analyse proportions with log-ratios;
- summarise many measurements at once with **PCA**;
- fit and interpret **mixed-effects models** when several worms come from the same mouse, and see how they change the conclusions;
- fit a **growth curve** over time and turn its parameters into biology: final size, and when growth is fastest.

**How long it takes.** Plan on about **7 to 9 hours**, spread over three sessions:

| Session | Sections | Topic |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Getting started (and Appendix A if you are new to R), 0 to 5 | R basics, tidy data, importing, quality control |
| 2 | 6 to 11 | The worms: growth, body plan, scaling, sex differences, PCA, stichosome number |
| 3 | 12 to 16 | The mice: worms within hosts, mixed models, growth curves; combined figure, exercises |

At the start of each new session, re-run the earlier code first (see *Run All Chunks Above* below), because R forgets everything when it is closed.

### Install R and RStudio (once)

1. Install **R** (version 4.1 or newer; the newest is best) from <https://cran.r-project.org>. Choose the installer for your operating system.
2. Install **RStudio Desktop** (free) from <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>. RStudio is the program you will work in. It runs R for you.
3. Open RStudio. If you already had R, check its version: type `R.version.string` in the *Console* pane (bottom left) and press Enter.

::: {.callout .callout-note}
::: {.callout-title}
Opening and running this tutorial
:::

1. Unzip the project folder, then double-click **`trichuris_morphometrics_tutorial.Rproj`**. RStudio opens with the project folder as the working directory, which is what the `data/` paths in the code expect.
2. In the *Files* pane, open **`trichuris_landmark_morphometrics_tutorial.Rmd`**.
3. Install the packages once (the code is in Section 1). RStudio may also offer to install `rmarkdown` and `knitr`.
4. Work through the tutorial in either of two ways:
   - **Step by step (recommended for learning):** read a section, then run each code chunk with the green play button, or `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter` with the cursor inside it. Outputs appear below each chunk.
   - **All at once:** click **Knit** to build the whole tutorial as an HTML file with every output and figure.
5. **Run the chunks in order.** Later chunks use objects made by earlier ones. If you skip a chunk, or come back after closing RStudio, use **Run > Run All Chunks Above** (`Ctrl + Alt + P`, or `Cmd + Option + P` on a Mac) with your cursor in the chunk you want to run next.
6. If you see `cannot open file 'data/...'`, R is not looking in the project folder. Open the `.Rproj` file again, and check that `getwd()` shows the folder that contains the `.Rproj` file (for example `morphometrics_tutorial-main` if you downloaded it from GitHub).
:::

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
Checking your figures and outputs
:::

Under every figure, and under the most important tables, there is a collapsed box (**"Check your figure"** or **"Check your output"**). Make your own plot first, then click the box to compare it with the expected result. Everyone uses the same data and the same random seeds, so your figure should match it exactly.

(If you are reading the **online version** of this tutorial, you won't see these boxes. The figures and tables on that page already *are* the expected results. They appear once you download the tutorial and run it yourself.)

- In the **knitted HTML**, the box sits just below your figure. Click it to open it.
- When you **run chunks one at a time** in RStudio, the expected figures are in the `expected_figures/` folder (*Files* pane), named after the chunk, for example `fig-growth.png`. Expected tables are written out in the `.Rmd` file itself, just below their chunk.

If yours looks different, check that you ran the earlier chunks in order and didn't change the code.
:::

### Appendices at the end

- **[Appendix A: R in ten minutes](#appendix-a-r-in-ten-minutes).** If you have never used R, work through this first (about 20 minutes). It covers the handful of ideas the code relies on: storing values with `<-`, vectors, functions, missing values (`NA`), tables (tibbles), factors, the pipe `|>` and short functions such as `\(x) x / 1000`. Come back here when you've finished.
- **[Appendix B: how to set out your own data table](#appendix-b-how-to-set-out-your-own-data-table).** How to lay out a spreadsheet so the analysis is easy: the template workbook, recommended columns and tidy-data habits. Read it before you enter your own data.
- **[Appendix C: how the practice data were simulated](#appendix-c-how-the-practice-data-were-simulated).** The R code behind the practice data. You don't need it for the tutorial; it is there for reference and for Exercise 6.

### When something goes wrong

Error messages in R look alarming but are usually one of a few things. Read the **last line** first.

| Message (or part of it) | What it usually means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `object 'worms' not found` | A chunk that makes `worms` hasn't been run in this session | **Run > Run All Chunks Above**, then run your chunk again |
| `could not find function "ggplot"` | The package isn't loaded | Run the `setup` chunk in Section 1 (the `library()` lines) |
| `there is no package called 'emmeans'` | The package isn't installed | Run the `install.packages()` line in Section 1 |
| `cannot open file 'data/...': No such file or directory` | R is looking in the wrong folder | Open the project by double-clicking the `.Rproj` file |
| `unexpected symbol` or `unexpected ')'` | A typo: a missing comma, bracket or quote | Compare your line character by character with the tutorial |
| `non-numeric argument to binary operator` | A column you did arithmetic on is text, not numbers | Look for text such as "250 um" or "n/a" in that column of the CSV |
| A `+` in the Console instead of `>` | R is waiting for you to finish a command (often an unclosed bracket) | Press `Esc`, then fix the code |

**Red text is not always an error.** R also prints **messages** (information, for example when a package loads) and **warnings** (something worth checking, but the code still ran) in red. Only text starting with `Error` means the code stopped. The knitted HTML hides messages and warnings to keep the page tidy, so you may see more red text when running chunks yourself than appears in the HTML.

If you are stuck, **Session > Restart R** and then **Run > Run All Chunks Above** fixes most problems caused by running things out of order.

## 0. Introduction and the practice data

In this tutorial you will analyse **body-axis measurements taken between anatomical landmarks** on whipworms (*Trichuris muris*) across the lifecycle. For each worm you may have measured whole-body length and the distances between structures such as the nerve ring and the entrance to the stichosome, and then asked:

- How does body length grow over time (days post infection, dpi)?
- How does the **body plan** (the proportion of the body occupied by each region) change between lifestages?
- Do body regions grow in proportion to the whole worm, or faster or slower (allometry)?
- Do males and females differ?
- How do we analyse all this when **each worm was only measured for a subset of the landmarks**?
- How do we handle the fact that **worms from the same mouse are not statistically independent**? (mixed-effects models)

All plots are made with **ggplot2**.

### How the data should be laid out

The analysis starts from a **tidy** table: **one row per worm, one column per variable, one value per cell**. Stage and sex go in separate columns, measurements are numbers in µm with the unit in the header, and a missing value is a blank cell (never 0, "-" or "n/a"). The practice data come as an untidy spreadsheet and as a tidy file. Section 3 looks at the problems in the untidy one, then reads the tidy one.

If you will be entering or preparing **your own data**, read [Appendix B: how to set out your own data table](#appendix-b-how-to-set-out-your-own-data-table). It covers the template workbook, the recommended columns, how to spot columns that need splitting, and good spreadsheet habits.

::: {.callout .callout-note}
::: {.callout-title}
About the Lifestage column in the practice file
:::

The practice file's `Lifestage` column has these values: "L1 – newly hatched", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4", "Adult – Female" and "Adult – Male". This is a common way lab sheets are kept. Two things to notice:

1. **"Adult – Female" combines two variables.** The tidy file has separate `lifestage` and `sex` columns. In future sheets, give each its own column, as the template does.
2. **"L1 – newly hatched" and "L1" are two groups in one column.** This tutorial treats them as separate groups. If "newly hatched" means hatched from eggs in vitro (not recovered from a mouse), those larvae have no host, which affects the mixed models (Sections 12 and 13). Record that in the `source` column.

Lab sheets also often end with a run of **blank rows**. The practice file has eight. If they are empty spreadsheet rows, they can be deleted. If they are worms whose lifestage wasn't recorded, the lifestage should be filled in. Section 3.2 checks which.
:::

### The simulated data structure

The simulated spreadsheet is laid out like a typical lab sheet. The tidy version, once prepared for analysis (Section 3.5), has **one row per worm** and these columns.

| Column (cleaned name) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dpi` | Days post infection (0 for newly hatched larvae) |
| `lifestage` | L1 (newly hatched), L1, L2, L3, L4, Adult female, Adult male |
| `stage`, `sex` | Stage and sex, split out of the original `Lifestage` label |
| `sample` | Replicate (worm) ID. Each sample is one independent worm |
| `host_id` | The mouse the worm came from. Worms from the same mouse share an ID. Blank for newly hatched larvae |
| `wb_length` | Whole-body length |
| `ant_nr` | Anterior end to nerve ring (NR) |
| `ant_st` | Anterior end to entrance of the stichosome (St) / end of oesophagus (Os) |
| `nr_st` | NR to entrance of St |
| `st` | Stichosome length |
| `intestine` | Intestine length |
| `ov_ts` | Ovary (females) / testis (males) |
| `rt_cl` | Rectum (females) / cloaca (males) |
| `rest` | Rest of body |
| `*_pct` | The same measurement as a percentage of whole-body length (calculated in R in Section 3.5, not recorded) |
| `st_number` | Approximate number of stichocytes (an estimate; about 50 to 60 at every stage) |

<details class="more-reading">
<summary>New to *Trichuris*? A short anatomy glossary (click to open)</summary>

- **Lifestages.** Four larval stages (L1 to L4), separated by moults, then adults. **dpi** is days post infection of the mouse.
- **Nerve ring (NR).** A ring of nerve tissue around the oesophagus, near the front of the worm. It is a convenient landmark.
- **Oesophagus (Os) and stichosome (St).** In whipworms, most of the oesophagus is surrounded by a column of large gland cells (**stichocytes**), together called the stichosome. It fills most of the long, thin front part of the worm (the "whip"). `st_number` is an approximate count of stichocytes. Unusually, this count stays roughly constant (about 50 to 60) through development: the stichosome grows because its cells get bigger, not more numerous (Section 11).
- **Intestine.** Runs through the thicker back part of the worm.
- **Ovary / testis (Ov/Ts)** and **rectum / cloaca (Rt/Cl).** Reproductive and terminal gut structures. Females have an ovary and a rectum, and males have a testis and a cloaca. The gonads only become visible in later larval stages.

The statistics in this tutorial don't depend on any of this. The same methods work for body regions of any animal.

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
::: {.callout-title}
Assumptions to check against your real data
:::

1. **Lengths are in µm.** If yours are in mm, only the axis labels change.
2. **Each row is one individual worm** (not a repeat measurement of the same worm). Worms that share a host are still *not statistically independent*, which is why the host ID matters (Sections 12 and 13).
3. **"L1 – newly hatched" larvae were hatched in vitro**, so they have `dpi = 0` and no host. If that is wrong for your data, find out which grouping they do belong to (for example a hatching batch) and use it in place of `host_id`.
4. **Each mouse is sampled at one timepoint** (mice are culled to collect worms), so mice are *nested within* dpi. Section 12 includes a check.
5. **The regions partition the body**, so the lengths add up to the whole-body length (and the `*_pct` columns calculated from them add up to about 100%). If your regions overlap (for example intestine running alongside the reproductive tract), they won't, and you should not treat the percentages as a composition. Section 5.3 tests this.
6. **The abbreviations** (NR = nerve ring, Os = oesophagus, St = stichosome, Int = intestine, Ov/Ts = ovary/testis, Rt/Cl = rectum/cloaca) are those used in this tutorial. Check that they match the ones used in your lab.
:::

::: {.callout .callout-note}
::: {.callout-title}
The simulated numbers are illustrative
:::

Sizes, proportions and mouse effects are invented to give realistic-looking patterns for teaching. They are **not real measurements**.
:::

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
Adding your real host column later
:::

If your data doesn't have a host column yet, you can still work through everything except Sections 12 and 13. The template already includes a `host_id` column. If you are rebuilding an existing sheet in the template layout, fill in `host_id` as you go. Columns are matched by **name**, not position, so nothing else needs changing.
:::

## 1. Setup

Install the packages once:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "patchwork", "emmeans", "lmerTest", "ggrepel", "rmarkdown", "knitr"))
```

(`lmerTest` also installs `lme4`, which fits the mixed models. `ggrepel` is used once, to stop labels overlapping in Section 10.)

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
Installing packages
:::

- Copy the line above into the **Console** (bottom-left pane) and press Enter. It can take **5 to 10 minutes** and prints a lot of text. That is normal.
- If R asks *"Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?"*, type `no` and press Enter. Installing "from sources" needs extra software you probably don't have.
- If R asks to update other packages, choosing **None** (or `n`) is fine.
- It has worked if `library(emmeans)` runs without an error. You never need to install again on this computer, but you do need the `library()` lines below in every session.
:::

Load them at the start of every session:

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)   # ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, readr, stringr ... in one go
library(patchwork)   # combine plots into multi-panel figures
library(lmerTest)    # mixed-effects models (loads lme4) with p-values
library(emmeans)     # model-based group means and contrasts (unbalanced data)

theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 12))

# Readable names for each body region, in anterior -> posterior order
segment_labels <- c(
  ant_nr    = "Anterior end to NR",
  nr_st     = "NR to St entrance",
  st        = "Stichosome",
  intestine = "Intestine",
  ov_ts     = "Ovary / testis",
  rt_cl     = "Rectum / cloaca",
  rest      = "Rest of body"
)

# Names of the matching percentage columns
pct_cols <- paste0(names(segment_labels), "_pct")
```

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
The pipe `|>`
:::

Read `|>` as "and then". `worms |> count(stage)` means "take `worms`, **and then** count the rows per stage". The short functions `\(x) ...` are explained in *R in ten minutes* ([Appendix A](#appendix-a-r-in-ten-minutes)).
:::

## 2. The practice data

The tutorial comes with **two practice CSV files** in a `data` folder. They are simulated (illustrative, **not real measurements**), and everyone uses the same files, so every student gets identical numbers and figures. Put the `data` folder in the same folder as this `.Rmd` file:

```
my_project/
  trichuris_landmark_morphometrics_tutorial.Rmd
  data/
    trichuris_muris_landmarks_messy.csv
    trichuris_muris_landmarks_tidy.csv
```

| File | What it is | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `trichuris_muris_landmarks_messy.csv` | A spreadsheet-style file, **untidy on purpose**, like a typical lab sheet. Section 3 looks at its problems | 238 rows x 22 columns (230 worms plus 8 empty rows) |
| `trichuris_muris_landmarks_tidy.csv` | The same 230 worms in the tidy layout of the template workbook. Sections 3.4 onward start from it | 230 rows x 16 columns |

The messy file contains the awkward features real data has:

- Lifestage labels in the format "L1 – newly hatched", "L1", ..., "Adult – Female", "Adult – Male", with a couple of stray trailing spaces.
- Newly hatched L1 larvae at 0 dpi, which come from no host (hatched in vitro).
- Other worms come from **mice** (4 to 5 mice per timepoint). Some mice carry larger or smaller worms, so worms from the same mouse resemble each other.
- Each worm was measured for only a **subset** of landmarks (length only, head landmarks only, or everything).
- Ovary/testis can't be measured in the youngest larvae (a **structural** missing value).
- A couple of **transcription errors** for you to find.
- Some **completely empty rows** at the bottom of the file.

::: {.callout .callout-note}
::: {.callout-title}
How the files were made
:::

Both files were generated by the script `tools/make_simulated_data.py` (fixed random seed 2026), so they can be regenerated exactly. The same design written in R is in [Appendix C](#appendix-c-how-the-practice-data-were-simulated) at the end, for reference and for Exercise 6. You don't need it for the tutorial.
:::


## 3. The raw spreadsheet: spotting problems

Lab sheets rarely arrive tidy. In this section we read the untidy practice file only to **look for problems**: empty rows, labels that combine two variables, missing values, and columns that could be calculated. We **don't fix them in R**. Converting an untidy sheet in code is fiddly and easy to get wrong, and the better fix is to set the data out tidily in the first place (see [Appendix B](#appendix-b-how-to-set-out-your-own-data-table)). The provided tidy file holds the same 230 worms already in that layout, and the rest of the tutorial uses it (Section 3.4).

### 3.1 Read the file and look at it

```{r import}
messy <- read_csv("data/trichuris_muris_landmarks_messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(messy)        # rows, columns
glimpse(messy)    # every column: its name, its type, and the first few values
```

Things to notice:

- **The headers are long sentences**, with spaces, brackets, slashes and dashes, such as `Anterior body end to NR`. R can use them, but only inside backticks (`` messy$`WB Length` ``), which is awkward to type. Short names such as `wb_length_um` are much easier.
- **Half of the columns are `% of Total` columns.** They can be calculated from the lengths, so they never need to be typed in, and they could disagree with the lengths if one is changed later.
- **Every measurement column is `<dbl>` (a number).** That is good: a single cell with text in it (for example "250 um" or "n/a") would turn the whole column into `<chr>` (text). Exercise 2 tries this.

### 3.2 Empty rows and inconsistent labels

How many rows are **completely** empty?

```{r messy-empty}
messy |>
  filter(if_all(everything(), is.na)) |>     # rows where every column is missing
  nrow()
```

Eight rows have nothing in them at all: blank rows left at the bottom of the spreadsheet. A row that was blank except for, say, a length would be a worm with no lifestage, which is a more serious problem. Checking that the rows are *entirely* empty tells the two apart.

Now count the labels in the `Lifestage` column:

```{r messy-labels}
messy |> count(Lifestage)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 8 × 2
  Lifestage              n
  <chr>              <int>
1 Adult – Female        55
2 Adult – Male          55
3 L1                    20
4 L1 – newly hatched    30
5 L2                    20
6 L3                    25
7 L4                    25
8 <NA>                   8
```

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- **"Adult – Female" holds two variables**, stage and sex, in one cell. To compare all adults regardless of sex, you would first have to pull them apart. The tidy file has separate `lifestage` and `sex` columns.
- **"L1 – newly hatched" and "L1" are two groups** of the same stage, differing in where the larvae came from. The tidy file records that in a `source` column.
- **The 8 `NA` labels** are the 8 empty rows.
- **Every spelling is its own group.** The file also has two labels with a stray space at the end. `read_csv()` removes leading and trailing spaces by default, so they don't appear here, but Excel and many other programs would treat "Adult – Female " as a different group. A `count()` like this is the quickest way to catch inconsistent labels.
:::

### 3.3 Missing values

How many cells are blank in each column?

```{r messy-missing}
messy |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>         # count the blanks in every column
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_missing")
```

Every column has at least 8 blanks: the empty rows. Beyond that, the blanks are **expected**. Each worm was measured for only some of the landmarks (length only, the head landmarks, or everything), and the ovary/testis can't be measured in young larvae. Section 4 looks at this pattern properly, worm by worm.

What you *can't* see by eye is the two **transcription errors** hidden in the file. They are ordinary-looking numbers. The quality-control checks in Section 5 find them.

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
What to take from this section
:::

Every problem above is easier to **prevent** than to fix. With the template workbook, drop-down lists stop inconsistent labels, stage and sex have their own columns, and percentages are never typed in. If you already have an untidy sheet, rebuilding it once in the template layout is usually quicker and safer than writing code to convert it. [Appendix B](#appendix-b-how-to-set-out-your-own-data-table) has the details.
:::

### 3.4 Read the tidy table

**From here on, everyone uses the provided tidy file**: the same 230 worms in the layout of the template workbook. It has short column names, separate `lifestage`, `sex` and `source` columns, lengths only (no percentages) and no empty rows. It still contains the two transcription errors, for Section 5 to find.

```{r read-tidy}
tidy <- read_csv("data/trichuris_muris_landmarks_tidy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(tidy)
```

If you entered your own data in the template workbook, this is your entry point: read your CSV instead.

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
Starting from your own template file
:::

```r
tidy <- read_csv("data/my_worms.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```
Optional columns (`batch`, `observer`, `measured_on`, `notes`) are fine to leave in or out. Everything below only uses the columns it needs.
:::

### 3.5 Prepare the analysis variables

Three jobs: strip the `_um` unit suffix to get short names for the code (the unit is recorded in the data dictionary), turn the categories into factors with a sensible order, and **calculate the percentages** that we chose not to record.

```{r tidy}
worms <- tidy |>
  rename_with(\(x) str_remove(x, "_um$")) |>        # wb_length_um -> wb_length, and so on
  mutate(
    # no `source` column? use  newly_hatched = dpi == 0
    newly_hatched = coalesce(source == "hatched in vitro", FALSE),

    stage = factor(lifestage, levels = c("L1", "L2", "L3", "L4", "Adult")),

    # one group label used in plots and models
    lifestage = case_when(
      newly_hatched                  ~ "L1 (newly hatched)",
      stage == "Adult" & !is.na(sex) ~ paste("Adult", str_to_lower(sex)),
      stage == "Adult"               ~ "Adult (sex unknown)",
      TRUE                           ~ as.character(stage)
    ),
    lifestage = factor(lifestage,
                       levels = c("L1 (newly hatched)", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4",
                                  "Adult female", "Adult male")),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Female", "Male"))
  ) |>
  # percentage of whole-body length, calculated rather than typed in
  mutate(across(c(ant_nr, ant_st, nr_st, st, intestine, ov_ts, rt_cl, rest),
                \(x) x / wb_length * 100, .names = "{.col}_pct"))

glimpse(worms)
```

```{r}
count(worms, dpi, lifestage, sex)
```

You now have the dataset used in every later section: `lifestage` (with sex folded in for adults), `stage`, `sex`, `host_id`, the lengths, and the calculated `*_pct` columns.

## 4. Look at what was measured (missingness)

With partial measurement, the first thing to do is see **who has which measurements**. This tells you which analyses are possible and how many worms each will use.

```{r miss-counts}
meas_cols <- c("wb_length", "ant_nr", "ant_st", "nr_st", "st",
               "intestine", "ov_ts", "rt_cl", "rest", "st_number")

# number of worms with a value, per stage
worms |>
  group_by(stage) |>
  summarise(n_worms = n(),
            across(all_of(meas_cols), \(x) sum(!is.na(x))),
            .groups = "drop")
```

A tile plot makes the pattern visible: one row per worm, one column per measurement, grey where a value exists.

```{r fig-missing, fig.height=6}
miss <- worms |>
  select(sample, stage, all_of(meas_cols)) |>
  arrange(stage, sample) |>
  mutate(sample = factor(sample, levels = sample)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(meas_cols), names_to = "measurement", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measurement = factor(measurement, levels = meas_cols),
         measured    = !is.na(value))

ggplot(miss, aes(x = measurement, y = sample, fill = measured)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey30", `FALSE` = "grey90"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Measured", `FALSE` = "Missing")) +
  facet_grid(stage ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Worms (grouped by stage)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x  = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-missing.png`.](expected_figures/fig-missing.png)

</details>

Reading the plot:

- `wb_length` is complete for everyone.
- Some worms have only the head landmarks (`ant_nr`, `nr_st`, `ant_st`), others only length, and others the full set.
- `ov_ts` is missing for all L1 (including newly hatched) and L2 worms. That is structural (the organ isn't there yet), not a gap.

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
Rule for the rest of the tutorial
:::

Every analysis uses **all the worms that have the measurements it needs**, and states how many that is. Don't throw away a worm because it lacks an unrelated measurement.
:::

## 5. Quality control

Do these checks **before** any plots or statistics.

### 5.1 Is `sample` a unique ID?

```{r qc-unique}
worms |>
  summarise(n_rows = n(), n_ids = n_distinct(sample), all_unique = n_ids == n_rows)
```

`all_unique` should be `TRUE` (230 rows and 230 IDs), confirming that each row is a different worm. If it is `FALSE`, the same ID appears on more than one row. Find out why before going further.

### 5.2 Do the distances add up?

`ant_st` (anterior end to St entrance) should equal `ant_nr` plus `nr_st`. Differences beyond rounding suggest a typing or measurement error.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** For every worm with all three head measurements, it works out how far `ant_st` is from `ant_nr + nr_st`, as a percentage of body length. Any worm more than 1% out is listed.

**Why it matters.** Statistics can't tell a real measurement from a typo. A single mistyped value (an extra digit, or two numbers swapped) can shift a group mean, make a slope look steeper, or create a "significant" difference that isn't there. Errors like this are cheap to catch now and expensive to discover after publication. Checks that use the data's own internal logic (parts that should add up, values that should be positive, IDs that should be unique) are the most reliable way to find them.
:::

```{r qc-arith}
worms <- worms |>
  mutate(err_ant_st_pct = (ant_st - (ant_nr + nr_st)) / wb_length * 100)

qc_flagged <- worms |>
  filter(abs(err_ant_st_pct) > 1) |>        # more than 1% of body length out
  select(sample, lifestage, wb_length, ant_nr, nr_st, ant_st, err_ant_st_pct)

qc_flagged
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  sample lifestage          wb_length ant_nr nr_st ant_st err_ant_st_pct
  <chr>  <fct>                  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>          <dbl>
1 S009   L1 (newly hatched)      231.   20.7  15.3   57.4           9.27
2 S078   L3                     1564.  132.  127.   414.            9.92
```

</details>

The two planted errors show up (samples S009 and S078 in the provided data). Never silently delete a suspicious worm. The best fix is to go back to the original measurement. If you can't, **flag the value and set it to `NA`**, keeping the worm's other measurements:

```{r}
worms <- worms |>
  mutate(
    ant_st_flag = coalesce(abs(err_ant_st_pct) > 1, FALSE),
    ant_st      = if_else(ant_st_flag, NA_real_, ant_st),
    ant_st_pct  = if_else(ant_st_flag, NA_real_, ant_st_pct)
  )
```

### 5.3 Do the regions make up the whole body?

Among fully measured worms, the percentage columns (calculated in R from the lengths) should sum to about 100. If they do, the regions you recorded add up to the whole-body length.

```{r qc-pct}
worms |>
  filter(!is.na(st_pct)) |>                          # fully measured worms
  mutate(pct_sum = rowSums(pick(all_of(pct_cols)), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  summarise(min = min(pct_sum), max = max(pct_sum))
```

Here they sum to ~100, so the regions partition the body. **If your real data does not, the regions overlap** (or a region is missing), and you should not analyse the percentages as parts of a whole.

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
Because the percentages are calculated from the lengths (Section 3.5), they can never disagree with them. This check is really testing the **lengths themselves**: do the regions you recorded add up to `wb_length`? That is why it is worth keeping.
:::

## 6. Growth: body length over time

::: {.callout .callout-note}
::: {.callout-title}
How the analysis is organised
:::

**Sections 6 to 11 focus on the worms**: growth, body plan, scaling, sex differences, PCA and stichosome number. They treat every worm as an independent observation, which is the simplest way to see the patterns.

**Sections 12 and 13 then bring in the mice.** Worms from the same mouse tend to resemble each other, so they are not fully independent. Section 12 shows this in the data, and Section 13 uses mixed-effects models to revisit the sex, growth and scaling comparisons while accounting for mouse. You will see which conclusions hold, and how much less certain some of them become. **Section 14** then fits a growth curve through all the timepoints, with mouse included.
:::

Every worm has `wb_length`, so this plot uses all of them.

```{r growth-table}
worms |>
  group_by(dpi, lifestage) |>
  summarise(n_worms = n(),
            n_mice  = n_distinct(host_id, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_um = mean(wb_length),
            sd_um   = sd(wb_length),
            .groups = "drop")
```

```{r fig-growth}
dpi_breaks <- worms |> distinct(dpi) |> pull(dpi)     # one axis tick per sampling day

p_growth <- ggplot(worms, aes(x = dpi, y = wb_length / 1000, colour = lifestage)) +
  # jitter x only (never jitter measurements); a fixed seed gives everyone the same picture
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, position = position_jitter(width = 0.8, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = dpi_breaks) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Days post infection (dpi)",
       y = "Whole-body length (mm, log scale)",
       colour = "Lifestage")

p_growth
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-growth.png`.](expected_figures/fig-growth.png)

</details>

A **log scale** is used because worms grow by orders of magnitude. On a linear axis the larvae would be squashed against the bottom. On the log scale, equal vertical distances mean equal fold-changes.

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Each dot is one worm, coloured by lifestage. Dots are spread a little sideways (jittered) so they don't hide each other. Their **height is never changed**.
- Worms grow about **130-fold**, from about 0.23 mm at hatching to about 29 mm in adult females at 42 dpi.
- Each larval step (L1 to L2, L2 to L3, L3 to L4) multiplies length by about 2.2 to 2.8 times. The biggest jump is from L4 (21 dpi) to adult (35 dpi), about 5.6-fold in females, over a longer gap of 14 days.
- At 35 and 42 dpi, adult females (yellow) sit above males (brown): females are longer. Section 9 looks at this properly.
:::

## 7. Body plan: how proportions change across lifestages

Which fraction of the body is stichosome, intestine and so on at each stage? A stacked bar of the mean percentages answers this. It uses fully measured worms only, and we show how many that is.

```{r fig-composition, fig.width=8}
comp <- worms |>
  filter(!is.na(st_pct)) |>                              # fully measured worms
  select(sample, lifestage, all_of(pct_cols)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(pct_cols), names_to = "segment", values_to = "pct") |>
  drop_na(pct) |>                                        # drops ov/ts in L1, L2
  mutate(segment = str_remove(segment, "_pct$"),
         segment = factor(segment, levels = names(segment_labels),
                          labels = segment_labels))

n_full <- worms |> filter(!is.na(st_pct)) |> count(lifestage)

comp_mean <- comp |>
  group_by(lifestage, segment) |>
  summarise(mean_pct = mean(pct), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(n_full, by = "lifestage") |>
  mutate(label = paste0(lifestage, "\n(n = ", n, ")"),
         label = fct_reorder(label, as.numeric(lifestage)))

p_comp <- ggplot(comp_mean, aes(x = label, y = mean_pct, fill = segment)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean % of whole-body length", fill = "Region") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))

p_comp
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-composition.png`.](expected_figures/fig-composition.png)

</details>

In the L1 and L2 groups the ovary/testis can't be measured, so that space is absorbed into "Rest of body". Interpret the early bars with that in mind. This figure is descriptive: any formal comparison of proportions between groups should also account for mouse (Section 13).

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Each bar is one group, and each coloured block is the **mean share** of body length taken by one region. The n under each bar is the number of fully measured worms behind it.
- The **stichosome's share rises** from about 38% in newly hatched L1 to about 54% in adults, while the **intestine's falls** from about 30% to about 17%. By adulthood the stichosome takes up more than half the body.
- The ovary/testis appears in L3 (about 2%). It reaches about 11% in adult females but only about 6% in males. Males make up the difference with a longer "rest of body" (about 12%, against 8% in females).
- These are means, so they hide the variation between worms. Exercise 3 models one of these percentages formally.
:::

### 7.1 Relative versus absolute length

Every bar above reaches 100%, so the plot shows the **shape** of the body plan but hides how **big** each worm is. Stacking the mean region lengths in mm (the same fully measured worms) shows the other half of the story. Adults are about 100 times longer than newly hatched L1 larvae, so on one shared axis the larvae would be invisible. We therefore give larvae and adults their own panel and axis.

```{r fig-composition-abs, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
comp_abs <- worms |>
  filter(!is.na(st_pct)) |>                              # the same fully measured worms
  select(sample, lifestage, stage, all_of(names(segment_labels))) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(names(segment_labels)), names_to = "segment", values_to = "length_um") |>
  drop_na(length_um) |>                                  # drops ov/ts in L1, L2
  mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = names(segment_labels),
                          labels = segment_labels)) |>
  group_by(stage, lifestage, segment) |>
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(length_um) / 1000, .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(n_full, by = "lifestage") |>
  mutate(label = paste0(lifestage, "\n(n = ", n, ")"),
         label = fct_reorder(label, as.numeric(lifestage)))

abs_bars <- function(d, title) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x = label, y = mean_mm, fill = segment)) +
    geom_col(colour = "white") +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", drop = FALSE) +   # same colours in both panels
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean length (mm)", fill = "Region", title = title) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))
}

p_abs <- abs_bars(filter(comp_abs, stage != "Adult"), "Larvae") +
  abs_bars(filter(comp_abs, stage == "Adult"), "Adults") +
  plot_layout(widths = c(5, 2))

# relative (top) above absolute (bottom), sharing one legend
(p_comp + labs(title = "Relative: % of whole-body length")) / p_abs +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-composition-abs.png`.](expected_figures/fig-composition-abs.png)

</details>

Read the two rows together:

- **Relative (top)**: the stichosome's *share* rises from about 38% to over 50%. The worm is changing shape.
- **Absolute (bottom)**: every region gets longer, by very different amounts. The stichosome grows from under 0.1 mm in a newly hatched L1 to over 10 mm in an adult female. The total height of each bar is the mean body length of these worms.
- A region can lose share while still growing in absolute length. The intestine does exactly that (compare its slope below 1 in Section 8).

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
Don't fix the size problem with a log axis. On a log scale each stacked segment's height no longer matches its length, so the stack becomes misleading. Use separate panels, as here, or plot each region on its own (Section 8).
:::

### 7.2 Percentages are parts of a whole

The percentages in Section 7 always add up to 100. That sounds harmless, but it means they are **not free to vary independently**: if one region's share goes up, the others *must* go down, whatever the biology. Data like these are called **compositional data**, and they need some care once you go beyond describing them.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**The problem.** Percentages have three quirks:

1. **They manufacture negative correlations.** Because the shares add to 100, they tend to be negatively correlated even when the regions themselves are completely unrelated. A negative correlation between two percentages can look like a biological trade-off ("worms with a bigger stichosome have a smaller intestine") when it is just arithmetic.
2. **They depend on what else is in the whole.** The stichosome's share changes if you add or remove another region from the total, even though the stichosome itself hasn't changed. In L1 and L2 the ovary/testis can't be measured and its space is absorbed into "rest of body" (Section 7), so the percentages of the early stages aren't strictly comparable with the later ones.
3. **They are squeezed between 0 and 100**, so their spread depends on their mean, which linear models don't expect.

**The fix: log-ratios.** Compare regions **with each other** as ratios, on the log scale. The ratio of stichosome to intestine doesn't care what else is in the body, and logs of ratios are unbounded. The most common version is the **centred log-ratio (CLR)**: each region's log length minus the worm's mean log length. That is exactly what Section 10.1 did to remove size, so you have already used it.

**Why it matters.** Body proportions are central to morphometrics, and percentages are the obvious way to express them. Used for description, as in the bars of Section 7, they are fine. Correlated or modelled, they can produce patterns that aren't there and hide ones that are. Compositional data analysis is standard in geology and microbiome studies, and less well known in morphometrics.
:::

**First, a demonstration with made-up numbers.** Three body regions whose lengths are drawn completely independently, so they have no relationship at all:

```{r comp-demo}
set.seed(1)
toy <- tibble(a = rlnorm(1000, log(10), 0.2),   # three independent lengths, each about 10
              b = rlnorm(1000, log(10), 0.2),
              c = rlnorm(1000, log(10), 0.2))

toy_pct <- toy / rowSums(toy) * 100               # each region as % of the total

round(cor(toy), 2)       # correlations between the lengths
round(cor(toy_pct), 2)   # correlations between the percentages
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
      a    b    c
a 1.00 0.01 0.05
b 0.01 1.00 0.02
c 0.05 0.02 1.00
      a     b     c
a  1.00 -0.52 -0.48
b -0.52  1.00 -0.50
c -0.48 -0.50  1.00
```

</details>

The lengths are uncorrelated (all about 0), as they should be. The percentages all correlate at about **−0.5**, purely because they must add to 100. With more regions the effect is weaker, but when one region dominates, as the stichosome does in adults, it is strong.

**Now the real data.** In adult females, how do the stichosome and intestine vary together?

```{r comp-cor}
worms |>
  filter(lifestage == "Adult female", !is.na(st_pct), !is.na(intestine_pct)) |>
  summarise(n_worms          = n(),
            cor_percentages  = cor(st_pct, intestine_pct),
            cor_lengths      = cor(log(st), log(intestine)))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  n_worms cor_percentages cor_lengths
    <int>           <dbl>       <dbl>
1      21          -0.745       0.426
```

</details>

The two correlations point in **opposite directions**. The lengths correlate positively (0.43): a bigger female tends to have both a longer stichosome and a longer intestine, simply because she is bigger. The percentages correlate negatively (−0.75), which would suggest a trade-off between the two organs. Most of that is the arithmetic from the demonstration: the stichosome takes up more than half the body, so a worm whose stichosome is a little longer than usual has every other share squeezed. A negative correlation between percentages is not, on its own, evidence of a trade-off.

**Comparing groups: percentages against log-ratios.** Do adult males and females differ in their body proportions? We test each region twice: once as a percentage, and once as a centred log-ratio. To keep the comparison fair, both use the same worms (adults with all seven regions measured), and both treat every worm as independent, as in Sections 6 to 11.

```{r comp-compare}
regions <- names(segment_labels)   # all seven regions, ov_ts included (adults have one)

adult_comp <- worms |>
  filter(stage == "Adult") |>
  drop_na(all_of(regions)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(regions), names_to = "region", values_to = "length_um") |>
  group_by(sample) |>                                         # within each worm:
  mutate(pct = 100 * length_um / sum(length_um),             #   % of the seven regions (adds to 100)
         clr = log(length_um) - mean(log(length_um))) |>     #   centred log-ratio
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = regions, labels = segment_labels))

sex_test <- function(d, response) {
  lm(reformulate("sex", response), data = d) |>   # e.g. pct ~ sex
    broom::tidy() |>
    filter(term == "sexMale") |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

adult_comp |>
  group_by(region) |>
  group_modify(\(d, key) bind_cols(
    sex_test(d, "pct") |> rename(pct_diff = estimate, pct_p = p.value),
    sex_test(d, "clr") |> rename(clr_diff = estimate, clr_p = p.value))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(pct_diff       = round(pct_diff, 2),
         male_vs_female = round(exp(clr_diff), 2),            # CLR difference as a ratio
         across(c(pct_p, clr_p), \(p) if_else(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.2g", p)))) |>
  select(region, pct_diff, pct_p, male_vs_female, clr_p)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 7 × 5
  region             pct_diff pct_p  male_vs_female clr_p 
  <fct>                 <dbl> <chr>           <dbl> <chr> 
1 Anterior end to NR     0.02 0.89             1.04 0.12  
2 NR to St entrance     -0.12 0.24             1    0.92  
3 Stichosome             0.5  0.62             1.04 0.21  
4 Intestine              0.67 0.19             1.08 0.0044
5 Ovary / testis        -5.76 <0.001           0.51 <0.001
6 Rectum / cloaca       -0.07 0.21             1    0.84  
7 Rest of body           4.77 <0.001           1.68 <0.001
```

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- `pct_diff` is how many **percentage points** larger the region's share is in males than in females. `male_vs_female` is the CLR difference as a **ratio**: how much longer the region is in males, relative to the worm's average region. 1.08 means 8% longer.
- **Both methods agree on the big differences.** Males have a much smaller testis than females have ovary (5.8 points less; a ratio of 0.51, about half), and a much longer rest of body (4.8 points more; a ratio of 1.68).
- **They disagree on the intestine.** As a percentage, the male intestine is 0.67 points larger, with p = 0.19: no evidence of a difference. As a log-ratio it is 8% longer, with p = 0.004. The simulation did build in a small real difference (males 19% of the body, females 18%, Appendix C), and the log-ratio picks it up while the percentage misses it.
- **But log-ratios need care too.** A CLR compares each region with the worm's *average* region. When the ovary/testis halves and the rest of body grows by two thirds, that average shifts, and every other region's CLR moves by about 3%. That is why the stichosome shows 1.04 even though the simulation gave it exactly the same share in both sexes. Part of the intestine's 8% is this shift. When your question is about one specific pair of regions, use a simple log-ratio such as `log(intestine / st)` (Exercise 8).

**In practice:** use percentages to **describe** a body plan (Section 7's bars), and log-ratios to **correlate, model or test** proportions. Always say what each ratio is relative to.
:::

## 8. Scaling: do regions grow in proportion to the whole worm?

If a region grows at the same rate as the whole body, its share stays constant. If it grows faster or slower, its share changes. This is **allometry**. On log-log axes, the slope of a region's length against whole-body length tells you which:

- **Slope = 1**: isometric (the region keeps its proportion)
- **Slope > 1**: the region gets proportionally larger as worms grow
- **Slope < 1**: the region gets proportionally smaller

This uses every worm that has the region measured (not just the fully measured ones).

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** For each region, it fits a **linear regression**: the straight line that best predicts region length from body length. "Best" means the line that makes the vertical distances between the points and the line as small as possible (least squares). The **slope** of the line says how much region length changes for each unit change in body length.

**Why use logs of both lengths?** Growth is multiplicative: a region that is always 40% of the body doubles when the body doubles. Biologists describe this with a **power law**, region = a × body^b. Taking logs of both sides turns it into a straight line, log(region) = log(a) + b × log(body), so the **slope of the log-log line is the exponent b**. A slope of 1 means the region keeps its proportion; above 1, it gets relatively bigger as the worm grows.

**Why it matters.** Percentages (Section 7) show *that* proportions change, but not *how fast* each region grows relative to the body. A slope with a confidence interval puts a number on it, and lets you test it against 1. Allometric slopes are the standard way to compare growth patterns between regions, stages, sexes or species, because they don't depend on the size of the animals you happened to measure.

**Confidence intervals.** A **95% confidence interval** is the range of values that are reasonably compatible with the data. If you repeated the whole study many times, about 95% of the intervals calculated this way would contain the true value. A narrow interval means the estimate is precise. If the interval excludes a value of interest (here, 1), the data give good evidence against that value.
:::

```{r fig-scaling, fig.height=6}
seg_cols <- names(segment_labels)

seg_long <- worms |>
  select(sample, any_of("host_id"), stage, wb_length, all_of(seg_cols)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(seg_cols), names_to = "segment", values_to = "length_um") |>
  drop_na(length_um) |>
  filter(length_um > 0) |>                                   # logs need positive values
  mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = names(segment_labels),
                          labels = segment_labels))

p_scaling <- ggplot(seg_long, aes(x = wb_length, y = length_um)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = stage), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  facet_wrap(~ segment, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Whole-body length (µm, log scale)",
       y = "Region length (µm, log scale)", colour = "Stage")

p_scaling
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-scaling.png`.](expected_figures/fig-scaling.png)

</details>

Extract the slope for each region, with a confidence interval.

::: {.callout .callout-note}
::: {.callout-title}
Advanced code: you don't need to follow every detail
:::

This chunk fits **one straight-line model per region** and collects the slopes into one table. What each line does:

1. `group_by(segment)` splits the long table into one group per region.
2. `group_modify(\(d, key) ...)` runs the same job on each group. Inside it, `d` is that region's rows.
3. `lm(log10(length_um) ~ log10(wb_length), data = d)` fits the line: region length against body length, both on log scales. Read `~` as "is modelled by".
4. `broom::tidy(..., conf.int = TRUE)` turns the model's results into a small table, with confidence intervals.
5. `filter(term == "log10(wb_length)")` keeps the slope row and drops the intercept row.

If you want to see one model on its own first, try `lm(log10(length_um) ~ log10(wb_length), data = filter(seg_long, segment == "Stichosome"))` in the Console.
:::

```{r scaling-slopes}
slopes <- seg_long |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  group_modify(\(d, key) broom::tidy(lm(log10(length_um) ~ log10(wb_length),
                                        data = d),
                                     conf.int = TRUE)) |>
  filter(term == "log10(wb_length)")

slopes |> select(segment, slope = estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 7 × 4
# Groups:   segment [7]
  segment            slope conf.low conf.high
  <fct>              <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Anterior end to NR 0.780    0.770     0.789
2 NR to St entrance  0.834    0.824     0.844
3 Stichosome         1.08     1.07      1.09 
4 Intestine          0.877    0.869     0.886
5 Ovary / testis     1.48     1.41      1.55 
6 Rectum / cloaca    0.834    0.822     0.847
7 Rest of body       0.982    0.961     1.00 
```

</details>

```{r fig-slopes, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(slopes, aes(x = estimate, y = fct_rev(segment))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  labs(x = "Scaling slope against whole-body length (isometry = 1)", y = NULL)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-slopes.png`.](expected_figures/fig-slopes.png)

</details>

Regions that gain share over development (here the stichosome) have a slope above 1, and regions that lose share (here the intestine) have a slope below 1.

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Each point is one region's slope. The horizontal line through it is the **95% confidence interval**: the range of slopes that fit the data well. The dashed line at 1 is isometry.
- If an interval does **not** cross the dashed line, that region clearly does not scale isometrically. Only "rest of body" (0.98, interval 0.96 to 1.00) is close to isometric.
- The steepest slope is the **ovary/testis (about 1.5)**: gonads barely exist in larvae and grow fast late in development. The **stichosome (1.08)** grows a little faster than the body, so it gains share.
- The head regions (anterior end to NR 0.78, NR to St 0.83), the intestine (0.88) and the rectum/cloaca (0.83) grow more slowly than the body, so they lose share. That is the same pattern as the stacked bars in Section 7, now with a number and an uncertainty attached.
- The intervals look very narrow because this analysis treats every worm as independent and pools all stages. See the cautions below.
:::

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
::: {.callout-title}
Three cautions
:::

1. **Parts of a whole are not independent.** The regions sum to the body length, so if one takes a bigger share, others must shrink. Don't over-interpret one slope in isolation.
2. **These slopes pool all lifestages.** They mix within-stage growth with the step changes between stages. To ask "does the region scale within adults?", repeat the model on one stage at a time.
3. **These confidence intervals ignore mouse.** Section 13.7 refits one slope with a mouse random effect.
:::

## 9. Sex differences in adults: look at the data

Males and females can only be compared in the adult stages. We start by plotting the data with n, then model it in Section 13.

```{r fig-sex}
adults <- worms |>
  filter(stage == "Adult") |>
  mutate(dpi_f = factor(dpi))

adults |>
  group_by(dpi, sex) |>
  summarise(n_worms = n(), n_mice = n_distinct(host_id), .groups = "drop")

sex_cols <- c(Female = "#C8553D", Male = "#2E86AB")

ggplot(adults, aes(x = sex, y = wb_length / 1000, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ dpi_f, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Whole-body length (mm)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-sex.png`.](expected_figures/fig-sex.png)

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- In a **boxplot**, the thick line is the **median** (the middle worm). The box holds the **middle 50%** of worms, and the whiskers reach the furthest worms that aren't unusually far out. The dots are the individual worms; the boxplot's own outlier points are switched off because every worm is already drawn.
- Females are longer at both timepoints: median about **24.8 mm against 19.1 mm** at 35 dpi, and **28.5 mm against 22.4 mm** at 42 dpi. Both sexes are longer at 42 dpi than at 35 dpi.
- The boxes for the two sexes hardly overlap, which suggests a clear difference. But this plot treats every worm as independent. Section 13 tests it while allowing for mouse.
:::

In this design, **both sexes come from each mouse**, so sex is compared *within* mice, while timepoint (35 vs 42 dpi) is compared *between* mice. This distinction matters when we model the sex difference while accounting for mouse in Section 13.

## 10. Multivariate analysis: PCA across lifestages

PCA summarises several region lengths at once, so we can see overall development and which regions drive it. **PCA needs complete rows**, so choose your variables with the missingness map in mind.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** Each worm has six region lengths, so it is a point in a six-dimensional space, which you can't draw. **Principal component analysis (PCA)** finds new axes through that cloud of points. The first, **PC1**, points in the direction along which the worms differ most. **PC2** is the direction of the next-largest difference, at right angles to PC1, and so on. Each PC is a weighted combination of the original measurements; the weights are called **loadings**. Plotting PC1 against PC2 is like turning the cloud until you find the most informative view of it.

**Why log and scale the data?** Logs make PCA about **proportional** differences, as in Section 8. **Scaling** (`scale. = TRUE`) gives every region the same weight. Without it, long regions such as the stichosome would dominate simply because their numbers are bigger.

**Why it matters.** Six measurements that are all strongly related carry much less than six separate pieces of information. PCA shows how many independent patterns there really are, which groups separate, and which measurements drive the separation, without running a separate test for every measurement. It is **descriptive**: it shows patterns but does not test them. To test whether groups differ on a PC, use the scores in a model (Exercise 4).
:::

Choices made here:

- Use the **region lengths** (not the `*_pct` columns, which carry the same information as the lengths, and not `wb_length` or `ant_st`, which are sums of the others).
- **Leave out `ov_ts`**, because it is structurally missing in L1 and L2. Including it would remove whole lifestages from the analysis.
- Use **log-transformed** lengths and scale them.

```{r pca}
pca_vars <- c("ant_nr", "nr_st", "st", "intestine", "rt_cl", "rest")

pca_data <- worms |>
  select(sample, any_of("host_id"), dpi, lifestage, stage, all_of(pca_vars)) |>
  drop_na(all_of(pca_vars))      # only the variables in the PCA: host_id may legitimately be NA

nrow(pca_data)                 # how many worms contribute?
count(pca_data, lifestage)     # ... and from which stages?
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
[1] 95
# A tibble: 7 × 2
  lifestage              n
  <fct>              <int>
1 L1 (newly hatched)    13
2 L1                     9
3 L2                     7
4 L3                    13
5 L4                    12
6 Adult female          21
7 Adult male            20
```

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
The PCA uses only the **fully measured subset**. Check that every lifestage is still represented in reasonable numbers, as above. If one stage vanished, conclusions about it would be impossible. Also avoid filling gaps with the mean: that shrinks variation and distorts the axes.

Note that `drop_na()` is restricted to the PCA variables. A bare `drop_na()` would also remove worms whose `host_id` is missing (the newly hatched larvae), which is not what we want here.
:::

```{r}
pca <- pca_data |>
  select(all_of(pca_vars)) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), log10)) |>
  prcomp(scale. = TRUE)

summary(pca)
```

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- **Standard deviation** is how spread out the worms are along each principal component (PC). **Proportion of Variance** is the share of all the variation that PC captures, and **Cumulative Proportion** is the running total.
- **PC1 captures 99.6%**. Almost all the variation among these worms is **size**: a big worm has big everything. That is expected when lengths span a 100-fold range.
- PC2 captures only 0.17%. It describes small differences in proportions, which is the shape. Section 10.1 removes size to look at shape directly.
:::

```{r fig-pca}
# share of the variation captured by each PC, as a tibble (columns PC, std.dev, percent, cumulative)
var_explained <- broom::tidy(pca, matrix = "eigenvalues")

pc_lab <- function(i) {
  share <- var_explained |> filter(PC == i) |> pull(percent)
  str_glue("PC{i} ({round(100 * share, 1)}%)")
}

scores <- bind_cols(pca_data |> select(sample, any_of("host_id"), dpi, lifestage),
                    as_tibble(pca$x))

p_pca <- ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = lifestage)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = pc_lab(1), y = pc_lab(2), colour = "Lifestage")

p_pca
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-pca.png`.](expected_figures/fig-pca.png)

</details>

Expect PC1 to be mostly **overall size**, ordering worms from L1 through adults, because all regions grow together. PC2 and later axes describe how the proportions differ.

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Each dot is one worm. Each ellipse encloses roughly 90% of a group, to show where most of its worms lie.
- **PC1** orders the worms by lifestage, from L1 (left) to adults (right): it is size. Newly hatched and 3 dpi L1 larvae overlap, because they are almost the same size.
- **PC2** separates adult males (above 0) from adult females (below). The loadings plot below shows why.
- The two axes are on very different scales: PC2 spans about 0.4 units and PC1 about 7. The plot stretches PC2 so you can see it.
- The direction of a PC is arbitrary: flipping its sign gives exactly the same analysis. If your plot is a **mirror image** of the expected one, that is fine.
:::

```{r fig-loadings, fig.height=4}
loadings <- as_tibble(pca$rotation, rownames = "region")
loadings

ggplot(loadings, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  # labels stacked to the right of the arrow tips, joined to them by thin lines
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = region),
                           nudge_x = 0.2, direction = "y", hjust = 0,
                           min.segment.length = 0, segment.colour = "grey60", seed = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.8, 0.9)) +
  labs(x = pc_lab(1), y = pc_lab(2))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-loadings.png`.](expected_figures/fig-loadings.png)

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Each arrow is one region. Its **loadings** (where the arrow points) say how much that region contributes to PC1 and PC2.
- All the arrows reach the same distance to the right: every region has a PC1 loading of about **0.41**. PC1 is all regions together, **overall size**.
- PC2 is dominated by **rest of body** (pointing up, 0.88), against the rectum/cloaca and the head regions (pointing down). A worm high on PC2 has a relatively long rest of body.
- Adult males have a longer rest of body than females (about 12% against 8%, Section 7), so males sit higher on PC2 in the score plot.
:::

### 10.1 Removing size to see shape only

Because size dominates PC1, shape differences are hidden in later axes. A simple way to focus on shape is to divide out size: subtract each worm's **mean log length** from every one of its log region lengths. What remains is the worm's relative proportions. (This is the centred log-ratio from Section 7.2.)

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** For each worm, it calculates one size number (the mean of its log region lengths) and subtracts it from every log length. Subtracting on the log scale is the same as dividing on the original scale, so what remains is each region **relative to the worm's overall size**. A PCA of these values describes shape only.

**Why it matters.** Separating **size** from **shape** is the central problem of morphometrics. Two worms can differ simply because one is bigger, or because their body plans really differ. Ordinary PCA mixes the two, and size usually swamps everything else, as PC1's 99.6% showed. Removing size first reveals the body-plan differences, such as stage and sex differences in proportions. Plotting shape against size then asks directly whether shape changes as worms grow.
:::

```{r fig-shape-pca, fig.width=9}
shape_data <- pca_data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(pca_vars), log),                      # log every region length
         log_size = rowMeans(pick(all_of(pca_vars))),         # one size number per worm
         across(all_of(pca_vars), \(x) x - log_size))         # subtract it: what's left is shape

shape_pca <- shape_data |>
  select(all_of(pca_vars)) |>
  prcomp()                            # the last PC will have ~zero variance: ignore it

shape_scores <- bind_cols(shape_data |> select(sample, any_of("host_id"), lifestage, log_size),
                          as_tibble(shape_pca$x))

p_shape1 <- ggplot(shape_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = lifestage)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Shape PC1", y = "Shape PC2", colour = "Lifestage")

p_shape2 <- ggplot(shape_scores, aes(x = log_size, y = PC1, colour = lifestage)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Size (mean log length)", y = "Shape PC1", colour = "Lifestage")

p_shape1 + p_shape2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-shape-pca.png`.](expected_figures/fig-shape-pca.png)

</details>

The right-hand panel asks: **does shape change with size?** A clear trend means development changes body proportions (allometry), not just size.

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- With size removed, shape PC1 captures about **83%** of the remaining variation and shape PC2 about **10%**. Run `summary(shape_pca)` to see this.
- **Left panel.** Shape PC1 still runs from larvae (left) to adults (right): body proportions change step by step through development. Shape PC2 separates adult females (above) from males (below).
- **Right panel.** Shape PC1 rises steadily with size (correlation about 0.96): bigger worms have a different shape. This is the allometry from Section 8 seen again. Run `shape_pca$rotation` to see that shape PC1 is mainly the stichosome (+0.71) and rest of body (+0.37) against the anterior end to NR (−0.48).
- Within the adults (top right), shape differs mainly by **sex**, not by size: most of the size-related change in shape happens between stages.
- As with any PCA, an axis may come out mirror-imaged on another computer. That doesn't change the interpretation.
:::

::: {.callout .callout-note}
PCA itself ignores mouse. To test group differences in PC scores while accounting for host, treat a PC score as the response in a mixed model, for example `lmer(PC1 ~ lifestage + (1 | host_id), data = filter(shape_scores, !is.na(host_id)))`. Section 13 introduces these models, and Exercise 4 tries this one.
:::

## 11. Stichosome number: a structure that grows without adding cells

In *Trichuris*, the number of stichocytes (the gland cells that make up the stichosome) is **set early and stays roughly constant**, at about 50 to 60, from larva to adult. Yet the stichosome itself grows more than a hundred times longer between newly hatched L1 and adult (Section 8). The question here is therefore the opposite of the scaling section: not *how fast* something grows, but whether it **changes at all**. Showing that something stays the same needs a little care, statistically.

`st_number` is an approximate count, recorded for a subset of worms from L2 onwards. First, the counts per lifestage and a plot against body size:

```{r fig-stnumber}
st_data <- worms |> drop_na(st_number)

st_data |>
  group_by(lifestage) |>
  summarise(n_worms = n(), median = median(st_number),
            min = min(st_number), max = max(st_number))

ggplot(st_data, aes(x = wb_length / 1000, y = st_number)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +  # straight line with its 95% CI band
  geom_point(aes(colour = lifestage), alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", drop = FALSE) +   # keep the same colours as the other figures
  expand_limits(y = c(40, 70)) +
  labs(x = "Whole-body length (mm, log scale)",
       y = "Approximate stichosome number", colour = "Lifestage")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-stnumber.png`.](expected_figures/fig-stnumber.png)

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Each dot is one worm. The black line is a straight-line fit, and the grey band around it is its 95% confidence interval.
- The medians sit between **54 and 57** in every group, from L2 to adults, while body length goes from under 1 mm to over 30 mm. The line is essentially flat.
- The spread within each group (about 48 to 60) is similar at every stage: worms differ a little in their count, but not in a way that depends on size.
- There are no L1 worms because stichosome number wasn't recorded for them. The L1 groups still appear in the legend so that the colours match the other figures.
:::

### 11.1 Is it really constant? Putting a number on "no change"

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** It fits a straight line of stichosome number against log10 body length, and reports the slope with its 95% confidence interval. The slope is the change in count for every **tenfold** increase in body length.

**Why not just look at the p-value?** A large p-value only says the data are compatible with no change. It doesn't say the change is zero: a small study with very noisy counts would give a large p-value even if the number doubled. "Not significant" is **absence of evidence**, not **evidence of absence**.

**What to look at instead.** The confidence interval. If the whole interval is close to zero, the data rule out any change big enough to matter. That *is* evidence that the number stays the same. (A formal version of this idea is called an **equivalence test**: you decide in advance how big a change would matter, and check that the interval falls entirely inside that range.)
:::

```{r stnumber-slope}
fit_st_number <- lm(st_number ~ log10(wb_length), data = st_data)

broom::tidy(fit_st_number, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "log10(wb_length)")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 log10(wb_length)   -0.833     0.720     -1.16   0.253    -2.28     0.612
```

</details>

The slope is **−0.8 stichocytes per tenfold increase in length**, with a 95% CI of **−2.3 to 0.6**. The worms here span about a 50-fold range of length (1.7 tenfold steps), so even the ends of the interval allow a change of only about 4 cells out of 55. The count is effectively constant.

### 11.2 So how does the stichosome grow?

If the number of stichocytes stays the same while the stichosome gets longer, each stichocyte must get longer. Divide stichosome length by stichosome number to get the average length per cell:

```{r stnumber-percell}
st_data |>
  drop_na(st) |>
  mutate(um_per_stichocyte = st / st_number) |>
  group_by(lifestage) |>
  summarise(n_worms           = n(),
            stichosome_um     = median(st),
            st_number         = median(st_number),
            um_per_stichocyte = median(um_per_stichocyte))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  lifestage    n_worms stichosome_um st_number um_per_stichocyte
  <fct>          <int>         <dbl>     <dbl>             <dbl>
1 L2                 6          294.      56                5.20
2 L3                 8          660.      54.5             11.7 
3 L4                11         2181       57               38.1 
4 Adult female      17        13442.      54              251.  
5 Adult male        13        11727.      56              211.  
```

</details>

From L2 to adult, the stichosome gets about **40 times longer** (about 0.3 mm to 12 to 13 mm), while the number of cells stays at about 55. The length per stichocyte rises from about **5 µm to over 200 µm**: the stichosome grows by **enlarging a fixed set of cells**, not by adding new ones.

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
Like the other analyses in Sections 6 to 11, this treats every worm as independent and ignores mouse. With only a few worms per stage it is a description, not a definitive test. Section 13 shows how to bring mouse into a model like this one.
:::

## 12. Worms within mice: the hierarchical structure

Every analysis so far (growth, body plan, scaling, sex differences, PCA and stichosome number) has treated each worm as an independent replicate. But the worms were collected from **mice**, and worms from the same mouse share a host environment (immune response, worm burden, how long the infection has run, diet and so on). That makes them more alike than worms from different mice.

### 12.1 How many mice, and how many worms per mouse?

```{r host-counts}
worms |>
  filter(!is.na(host_id)) |>
  count(dpi, host_id) |>
  group_by(dpi) |>
  summarise(n_mice        = n_distinct(host_id),
            n_worms       = sum(n),
            min_per_mouse = min(n),
            max_per_mouse = max(n))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 6 × 5
    dpi n_mice n_worms min_per_mouse max_per_mouse
  <dbl>  <int>   <int>         <int>         <int>
1     3      4      20             4             7
2     9      4      20             4             6
3    14      5      25             3             7
4    21      5      25             3             8
5    35      5      60             9            14
6    42      5      50             5            14
```

</details>

Notice how few mice there are at each timepoint compared with the number of worms. **The number of mice, not the number of worms, is what limits how confidently you can compare timepoints.**

Some worms have no host at all. Check which:

```{r}
worms |> filter(is.na(host_id)) |> count(dpi, lifestage)
```

These are the newly hatched larvae, which were hatched in vitro. They cannot be given a mouse random effect, and **mixed-effects models silently drop rows with a missing grouping variable**. In Section 13 we therefore filter them out explicitly, so you can see which worms each model uses. (If they share a hatching batch, a `batch` column could serve as their grouping variable instead.)

### 12.2 Is each mouse sampled at only one timepoint?

The models in Section 13 assume mice are *nested* within timepoints (each mouse contributes to a single dpi). Check that this holds:

```{r host-nesting}
worms |>
  filter(!is.na(host_id)) |>
  group_by(host_id) |>
  summarise(n_dpi = n_distinct(dpi)) |>
  filter(n_dpi > 1)             # should return zero rows
```

Zero rows means the nesting is clean. If your real design has mice contributing at several timepoints, the model structure changes (see Section 17).

### 12.3 Do mice differ from each other?

To see mouse-to-mouse variation across all stages on one axis, express each worm's length **relative to the average for its lifestage and timepoint** (1 = typical). If worms were independent, each mouse's worms would scatter evenly around 1.

```{r fig-mouse-clustering, fig.width=10}
worms <- worms |>
  group_by(dpi, lifestage) |>
  mutate(rel_length = wb_length / mean(wb_length)) |>
  ungroup()

worms |>
  filter(!is.na(host_id)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = host_id, y = rel_length)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = lifestage), alpha = 0.7,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, fun.min = mean, fun.max = mean,
               geom = "crossbar", width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.3) +   # mean per mouse
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", drop = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ dpi, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x", labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Mouse", y = "Body length relative to lifestage average", colour = "Lifestage") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-mouse-clustering.png`.](expected_figures/fig-mouse-clustering.png)

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
