How to read this
:::

- Each column is one mouse, and each dot is one of its worms. Panels are timepoints (dpi).
- The y-axis is each worm's length divided by the average for its lifestage and timepoint: **1** (dashed line) is average, **1.2** means 20% longer than average, and **0.8** means 20% shorter.
- The short horizontal bar is the **mean for that mouse**. If mice didn't matter, every bar would sit close to 1.
:::

Some mice have all their worms above 1 and others below. This is **clustering**: knowing which mouse a worm came from tells you something about its size. Ignoring that treats, say, 25 worms from 5 mice as if they were 25 independent pieces of evidence. This error is called **pseudoreplication**, and it makes confidence intervals too narrow and p-values too small.

## 13. Mixed-effects models: accounting for host

### 13.1 The idea

An ordinary linear model (`lm`) assumes every observation is independent. A **mixed-effects model** adds a **random effect** that says "observations from the same mouse share a mouse-specific shift":

- **Fixed effects** are the things you want to estimate and compare: sex, timepoint, body length.
- **Random effects** describe grouping structure you want to account for but are not interested in comparing mouse by mouse. Here, mouse.

In R's `lme4` syntax, `(1 | host_id)` means "a separate baseline (intercept) for each mouse, drawn from a common distribution". The model then splits variation into **between-mouse** and **within-mouse** components.

### 13.2 Fit the models

We model the **log** of length, so effects are ratios ("females are 25% longer"). We fit the ordinary model and the mixed model side by side.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What a linear model does.** `lm()` predicts a response (here log length) from one or more **predictors** (here sex and timepoint). The formula `sex * dpi_f` is shorthand for `sex + dpi_f + sex:dpi_f`: an effect of sex, an effect of timepoint, and an **interaction** (does the sex difference depend on timepoint?). The model estimates each effect and its standard error, and gives a p-value for each.

**What the mixed model adds.** `lmer()` fits the same model, plus `(1 | host_id)`: every mouse gets its own baseline. The model then knows which worms share a mouse, so it can separate variation between mice from variation within mice.

**Why log length?** Differences between groups in body size are usually proportional (females 25% longer), not fixed amounts (females 5 mm longer), and larger groups usually vary more. On the log scale both problems go away: effects become ratios, and the spread is similar across groups, which the model assumes.

**Why it matters.** Treating 110 worms from 10 mice as 110 independent animals overstates how much evidence you have. Standard errors come out too small, and p-values too small, especially for anything compared *between* mice, such as timepoint. That is how false "significant" results get published. A mixed model gives each comparison the precision its design really supports. Most reviewers now expect one whenever animals are nested within hosts, cages or batches.

**p-values.** A **p-value** is the probability of seeing an effect at least this large if there were really no effect. A small p-value (conventionally below 0.05) means the data would be surprising under "no effect". It does **not** tell you how big or important the effect is. Report the estimate and its confidence interval as well, which is what the rest of this section does.
:::

```{r lmm-fit}
fit_lm  <- lm(log(wb_length) ~ sex * dpi_f, data = adults)
fit_lmm <- lmer(log(wb_length) ~ sex * dpi_f + (1 | host_id), data = adults)

summary(fit_lmm)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```

lmerModLmerTest]
Formula: log(wb_length) ~ sex * dpi_f + (1 | host_id)
   Data: adults

REML criterion at convergence: -209.7

Scaled residuals: 
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.19444 -0.73063  0.03932  0.57932  2.67815 

Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 host_id  (Intercept) 0.004584 0.06771 
 Residual             0.006075 0.07794 
Number of obs: 110, groups:  host_id, 10

Fixed effects:
                Estimate Std. Error       df t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     10.12126    0.03351  9.28581 302.013   <2e-16 ***
sexMale         -0.24907    0.02063 99.15110 -12.075   <2e-16 ***
dpi_f42          0.15226    0.04790  9.66897   3.179   0.0103 *  
sexMale:dpi_f42  0.01405    0.03063 99.51422   0.459   0.6475

Correlation of Fixed Effects:

sexMale     -0.303

```

</details>

The "Random effects" block shows the **variance between mice** (`host_id`) and the leftover **residual variance** (worm-to-worm variation within a mouse).

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

This is the most information-dense output in the tutorial. Take it one block at a time.

**Random effects.** The variance between mice is 0.0046 and the residual (within-mouse) variance is 0.0061. Section 13.4 turns these into one number, the ICC.

**Fixed effects.** There is one row per term. Because we modelled **log(length)**, each estimate is a difference on the log scale. Applying `exp()` turns it into a **ratio**, which is easier to talk about.

| Row | Estimate | What it means | As a ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(Intercept)` | 10.12 | Predicted log length for the **reference group**: females at 35 dpi (R uses the first level of each factor as the reference) | exp(10.12) ≈ 24,900 µm, so about 24.9 mm |
| `sexMale` | −0.249 | Males compared with females, at 35 dpi | exp(−0.249) = 0.78: males are about **22% shorter** |
| `dpi_f42` | 0.152 | Females at 42 dpi compared with 35 dpi | exp(0.152) = 1.16: about **16% longer** |
| `sexMale:dpi_f42` | 0.014 | The **interaction**: does the sex difference change between 35 and 42 dpi? | Tiny, and p = 0.65: **no evidence** that it changes |

**The columns.** `Std. Error` is how precisely each estimate is known (smaller is more precise). `t value` is the estimate divided by its standard error. `Pr(>|t|)` is the p-value. `df` (degrees of freedom) is worth a closer look: `sexMale` has about 99, close to the number of **worms**, but `dpi_f42` has only about 10, close to the number of **mice**. That is the model recognising that timepoints are compared between mice, so only the mice count as replicates.

The "Correlation of Fixed Effects" block at the bottom can be ignored for now.

To see every fixed effect as a ratio at once, run `exp(fixef(fit_lmm))`.
:::

### 13.3 How does accounting for mouse change the answers?

```{r lmm-se}
# coef(summary(...)) is the model's coefficient table; as_tibble() makes it a tibble
se_lm   <- coef(summary(fit_lm))  |> as_tibble(rownames = "term") |> select(term, se_lm   = `Std. Error`)
se_lmer <- coef(summary(fit_lmm)) |> as_tibble(rownames = "term") |> select(term, se_lmer = `Std. Error`)

se_compare <- left_join(se_lm, se_lmer, by = "term")
se_compare
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  term             se_lm se_lmer
  <chr>            <dbl>   <dbl>
1 (Intercept)     0.0181  0.0335
2 sexMale         0.0256  0.0206
3 dpi_f42         0.0268  0.0479
4 sexMale:dpi_f42 0.0379  0.0306
```

</details>

What to expect, and why:

- **`sexMale`** is compared *within* each mouse. Removing between-mouse variation from the comparison usually makes the standard error **smaller** under the mixed model.
- **`dpi_f42`** is compared *between* mice (different mice at 35 and 42 dpi). The mixed model usually gives a **larger** standard error, because the real replication is the number of mice. The ordinary model was overconfident.

So a mixed model is not simply "more conservative". It gives each comparison the precision its design really deserves.

Now estimate the female/male ratio at each timepoint under both models:

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** `emmeans()` (estimated marginal means) asks a fitted model for its **predicted mean for each group**, with a confidence interval. Here it gives the predicted mean log length for each sex at each timepoint. `pairs()` then compares the sexes within each timepoint, and `type = "response"` converts the answer from the log scale back to a ratio (female ÷ male).

**Why not just use the raw group means?** Raw means ignore the model. They don't know that worms from the same mouse are related, so their standard errors are wrong. With **unbalanced** data (different numbers of worms per mouse or per group), they can also be pulled towards whichever mice contributed the most worms. Model-based means use the whole model, so their intervals reflect the real design.

**Why it matters.** Biologists usually want an answer like "females are 27% longer (95% CI 23 to 34%)" rather than a coefficient table. `emmeans` produces exactly that, from the right model, and handles the back-transformation from logs for you.
:::

```{r lmm-contrasts}
sex_ratio <- function(model, label) {
  emmeans(model, ~ sex | dpi_f, lmer.df = "satterthwaite") |>   # lmer.df is ignored for lm
    pairs() |>
    summary(type = "response", infer = TRUE) |>   # back-transform from log to ratio
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(model = label)
}

bind_rows(sex_ratio(fit_lm,  "lm (ignores mouse)"),
          sex_ratio(fit_lmm, "lmer (mouse random effect)")) |>
  select(model, dpi_f, contrast, ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  model                      dpi_f contrast      ratio lower.CL upper.CL
  <chr>                      <fct> <fct>         <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 lm (ignores mouse)         35    Female / Male  1.28     1.21     1.34
2 lm (ignores mouse)         42    Female / Male  1.27     1.20     1.35
3 lmer (mouse random effect) 35    Female / Male  1.28     1.23     1.34
4 lmer (mouse random effect) 42    Female / Male  1.26     1.21     1.32
```

</details>

A ratio of 1.25 means females are 25% longer than males. Compare the confidence intervals between the two models.

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- Both models give almost the same ratio: about **1.27**, so females are roughly 27% longer than males at both timepoints.
- The mixed model's intervals are slightly **narrower** (for example 1.23 to 1.34 against 1.21 to 1.34 at 35 dpi). That is what Section 13.3 predicted: sex is compared *within* mice, so removing the mouse-to-mouse variation sharpens the comparison.
- Both intervals are far from 1 (no difference), so the sex difference is clear whichever model you use.
:::

### 13.4 How much variation is between mice? (ICC)

The **intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)** is the proportion of total variation that is between mice. An ICC near 0 means worms from the same mouse are no more alike than worms from different mice. A high ICC means mouse matters a lot.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** It takes the two variances from the model's "Random effects" block and divides the between-mouse variance by the total: ICC = mouse variance ÷ (mouse variance + residual variance).

**Why it matters.** The ICC tells you how much the clustering matters, and so how to design the next experiment. With a high ICC, extra worms from the same mice add little information: the worms mostly repeat what their mouse already told you. To gain precision you need **more mice**. With an ICC near 0, worms behave almost independently, and measuring more worms per mouse is nearly as good as adding mice. Reporting the ICC also lets other researchers plan their sample sizes.
:::

```{r lmm-icc}
VarCorr(fit_lmm) |>
  as_tibble() |>                       # one row per variance component: host_id, Residual
  summarise(icc = round(vcov[grp == "host_id"] / sum(vcov), 2))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 1 × 1
    icc
  <dbl>
1  0.43
```

</details>

In the simulation, mouse and individual variation were set to similar sizes, so the ICC should be moderate. Here it is **0.43**: after allowing for sex and timepoint, 43% of the variation in adult length is between mice, and 57% is between worms from the same mouse. With real data, a high ICC means pseudoreplication would have been a serious problem.

### 13.5 Check the model

Two quick checks: the residuals should form an even cloud, and the mouse effects should be roughly normally distributed.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** Every model makes assumptions about the data. For this one: the leftover variation (the **residuals**) is roughly normal and has a similar spread everywhere, and the mouse effects are roughly normal. These plots let you see whether that is reasonable.

**Why it matters.** The standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values are only trustworthy if the assumptions roughly hold. A model can run without any error message and still give misleading answers, for example if one group is far more variable than the others or a few extreme values dominate. Checking takes a minute, and it is what a careful reviewer will ask about.
:::

```{r fig-lmm-diag, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
diag_df <- tibble(fitted = fitted(fit_lmm), resid = resid(fit_lmm))
re_df   <- ranef(fit_lmm) |> as_tibble() |> rename(effect = condval)   # one row per mouse

p_d1 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals", title = "Residuals vs fitted")

p_d2 <- ggplot(re_df, aes(sample = effect)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Mouse effects", title = "Mouse effects")

p_d1 | p_d2
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-lmm-diag.png`.](expected_figures/fig-lmm-diag.png)

</details>

With only a handful of mice, the mouse-effect plot will always look rough. Look for gross problems, not perfection.

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- **Left (residuals against fitted values).** Each dot is one worm. Its residual is how far its actual value is from the model's prediction. You want an **even band around 0 with no pattern**, as here. The vertical stripes are normal: worms of the same sex from the same mouse share a fitted value.
- Warning signs: a **funnel** (spread growing with the fitted value, which often means the data need a log scale), a **curve** (the model is missing something), or a few points **far from the rest** (check those worms in the data).
- **Right (Q-Q plot of mouse effects).** Each dot is one mouse (10 here). If the mouse effects are roughly normally distributed, the dots lie near the line. Here they do. With 10 points, small wiggles mean nothing: look for one mouse far off the line.
:::

### 13.6 More worms per mouse is not more mice

Back to growth. We compare estimated mean length for each lifestage-and-timepoint group with and without the mouse random effect. **First remove worms with no host** (the newly hatched larvae), so that both models use exactly the same rows. Otherwise `lmer` would drop them silently and the two models would not be comparable.

```{r lmm-growth}
worms_g <- worms |>
  filter(!is.na(host_id)) |>                       # same rows for both models
  arrange(dpi, lifestage) |>
  mutate(group = paste0(lifestage, ", ", dpi, " dpi"),
         group = factor(group, levels = unique(group)))

fit_g_lm  <- lm(log(wb_length) ~ group, data = worms_g)
fit_g_lmm <- lmer(log(wb_length) ~ group + (1 | host_id), data = worms_g)

est <- bind_rows(
  emmeans(fit_g_lm,  ~ group) |> summary(type = "response") |> as_tibble() |>
    mutate(model = "lm (ignores mouse)"),
  emmeans(fit_g_lmm, ~ group, lmer.df = "satterthwaite") |> summary(type = "response") |> as_tibble() |>
    mutate(model = "lmer (mouse random effect)")
)
```

The groups differ in size by a factor of 100, so on one shared axis every interval would shrink to a dot. Give each group its own panel and y-axis instead, so you can compare the **widths** of the two intervals:

```{r fig-lmm-growth, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
ggplot(est, aes(x = model, y = response / 1000,
                ymin = lower.CL / 1000, ymax = upper.CL / 1000, colour = model)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  facet_wrap(~ group, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) +   # each group gets its own y-axis
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey50", "#B5322B")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimated mean length (mm)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x  = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-lmm-growth.png`.](expected_figures/fig-lmm-growth.png)

</details>

In every panel the mixed-model interval (red) is wider. With only 4 to 5 mice per timepoint, a mean based on 20 to 30 worms is really supported by 4 to 5 independent mice, and the wider interval reflects that. **To narrow it, you need more mice, not more worms per mouse.**

### 13.7 A scaling slope with a mouse random effect

Back to allometry (Section 8). Here is the stichosome slope fitted with and without a mouse random effect, again using the same rows (worms with a host) for both:

```{r lmm-slope}
st_only <- seg_long |>
  filter(segment == "Stichosome", !is.na(host_id))

fit_st_lm  <- lm(log10(length_um) ~ log10(wb_length), data = st_only)
fit_st_lmm <- lmer(log10(length_um) ~ log10(wb_length) + (1 | host_id), data = st_only)

slope_row <- function(model, label) {
  estimates <- coef(summary(model)) |> as_tibble(rownames = "term")
  intervals <- confint(model, method = "Wald") |> as_tibble(rownames = "term")   # lm() ignores `method`

  left_join(estimates, intervals, by = "term") |>
    filter(term == "log10(wb_length)") |>
    transmute(model = label, slope = Estimate, conf.low = `2.5 %`, conf.high = `97.5 %`)
}

bind_rows(slope_row(fit_st_lm,  "lm (ignores mouse)"),
          slope_row(fit_st_lmm, "lmer (mouse random effect)"))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  model                      slope conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 lm (ignores mouse)          1.08     1.08      1.09
2 lmer (mouse random effect)  1.08     1.07      1.09
```

</details>

In the simulation, mice differ in their relative stichosome length, so worms from the same mouse share a stichosome offset that body length doesn't explain. Even so, the two slopes here are almost identical (about 1.08), and the mixed-model interval is only slightly wider. That is because body length spans about three orders of magnitude, from L1 to adult, so the slope is pinned down by the huge size range and a small mouse offset barely moves it. The mouse effect matters much more when the size range is narrow, for example within one stage (try Exercise 5).

### 13.8 Practical notes

- **Report both counts.** State the number of worms *and* the number of mice per group (for example "n = 25 worms from 5 mice").
- **Missing grouping values.** `lmer` silently drops rows where the grouping variable is `NA`. Filter them out yourself, as above, and say how many worms were excluded.
- **"Singular fit" warnings** mean the model estimated the between-mouse variance as essentially zero. Often this just means there is too little mouse-to-mouse variation or too few mice to estimate it. The ordinary model may then be adequate, but keeping the random effect is still the honest description of the design.
- **Few mice.** Random-effect variances are poorly estimated with fewer than about five mice per group. Interpret them cautiously.
- **Degrees of freedom.** `lmerTest` and `emmeans` use approximations (Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger) that reflect the number of mice. Report which was used. This tutorial sets `lmer.df = "satterthwaite"` in `emmeans()` so that everyone gets the same numbers: otherwise `emmeans` picks Kenward-Roger when the `pbkrtest` package happens to be installed, and Satterthwaite (with a message) when it isn't.
- **Write the model down.** For example: "log body length ~ sex × timepoint + (1 | mouse), fitted with lme4 and lmerTest in R".

## 14. Growth curves: modelling length over time

Section 6 described growth one sampling day at a time, and Section 13.6 estimated a mean for each group. Neither says anything about **between** the sampling days, or gives a single summary of how the worms grow. A **growth curve** does: it fits one smooth line through all the timepoints, and its parameters are things a biologist wants to know, such as the final adult size and when growth is fastest.

### 14.1 The idea

On a log scale (Section 6), body length follows an S-shape over time: slow in the first days, fastest in the middle of larval development, then levelling off in adults. A **logistic curve** has exactly that shape. On the log scale it has four parameters:

| Parameter | What it is | Read from the plot in Section 6 |
|---|---|---|
| `lo` | The lower plateau, the size the curve levels off towards on the left | below the L1 larvae: log(200 µm) ≈ 5.3 |
| `hi` | The upper plateau: **final adult size** | about adult size: log(30,000 µm) ≈ 10.3 |
| `xmid` | The day half way between the plateaus, when **relative growth is fastest** | somewhere around 20 dpi |
| `scal` | How spread out growth is in time: larger means slower, more drawn-out growth | about 5 days |

We add one more parameter, `male_diff`, which lowers the upper plateau for males. Larvae can't be sexed, so they all sit on the same curve, and the sex difference is estimated from the adults.

::: {.callout .callout-why}
::: {.callout-title}
What this analysis does, and why it matters
:::

**What it does.** It fits a **nonlinear model**: the curve's shape is fixed in advance (here, logistic), and R finds the parameter values that bring the curve closest to the data (least squares, as for a straight line). Unlike `lm()`, there is no formula for the answer, so R searches step by step, starting from **starting values** that you supply. Then it fits the same curve with a mouse random effect, just as `lmer()` did in Section 13.

**Why it matters.** The parameters summarise the whole growth trajectory in a few numbers with confidence intervals: "females level off at about 45 mm, males about 23% shorter, and relative growth peaks at about 14 dpi". These numbers can be compared directly between groups, for example between mouse strains, or treated and untreated mice, which is often the real question. The curve also gives the **growth rate** at any day, including days you didn't sample.

**The catch.** A curve is only as good as the timepoints behind it. Anything it says beyond your last sampling day is an **extrapolation**, and the upper plateau usually is one (Section 14.5).
:::

We use the worms with a mouse (`worms_g` from Section 13.6), so the newly hatched larvae are left out, and add a 0/1 column for males:

```{r gc-data}
# the logistic curve on the log scale, written as an R function
growth_curve <- function(dpi, lo, hi, xmid, scal) {
  lo + (hi - lo) / (1 + exp((xmid - dpi) / scal))
}

gc_data <- worms_g |>
  mutate(male = as.numeric(sex %in% "Male"))   # 1 for adult males, 0 for everyone else
```

### 14.2 Fit the curve, ignoring mouse

`nls()` fits a nonlinear model by least squares. The formula says: log length follows `growth_curve()`, with the upper plateau lowered by `male_diff` for males. `start` gives the starting values read off the Section 6 plot (in the table above).

```{r gc-nls}
fit_gc_nls <- nls(log(wb_length) ~ growth_curve(dpi, lo, hi + male_diff * male, xmid, scal),
                  data  = gc_data,
                  start = c(lo = 5.3, hi = 10.3, xmid = 20, scal = 5, male_diff = -0.25))
coef(fit_gc_nls)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
       lo        hi      xmid      scal male_diff 
 4.4865922 10.5837058 15.2919063  8.6310004 -0.2355828 
```

</details>

The starting values were rough, but the fit moved well away from them: `xmid` from 20 to about 15 days, `scal` from 5 to about 9. That is normal. Starting values only need to be close enough for R to find its way.

::: {.callout .callout-tip}
::: {.callout-title}
If the fit fails
:::

`nls()` can stop with errors such as `singular gradient` or `step factor reduced below minFactor`. These almost always mean the starting values are too far off, or the curve has more parameters than the data can support. Plot the data, read better starting values off the plot, and try again. If it still fails, try a simpler curve. **Always plot the fitted curve over the data** (Section 14.4): a curve can converge and still be nonsense.
:::

### 14.3 Add the mouse

As in Section 13, worms from the same mouse resemble each other. `nlme()` from the **nlme** package (installed with R, so there is nothing new to install) fits nonlinear **mixed** models. We add a parameter `mouse`, a random shift of log length for each mouse, which is the same "each mouse has its own baseline" idea as `(1 | host_id)`. The estimates from `nls()` are the starting values.

```{r gc-nlme}
fit_gc <- nlme::nlme(log(wb_length) ~ growth_curve(dpi, lo, hi + male_diff * male, xmid, scal) + mouse,
                     data   = gc_data,
                     fixed  = lo + hi + xmid + scal + male_diff ~ 1,   # one value of each for everyone
                     random = mouse ~ 1 | host_id,                     # a shift for each mouse
                     start  = coef(fit_gc_nls))

nlme::intervals(fit_gc, which = "fixed")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
Approximate 95% confidence intervals

 Fixed effects:
               lower       est.      upper
lo         3.3368237  4.0937149  4.8506060
hi        10.4745987 10.7174892 10.9603797
xmid      12.5540939 14.4966223 16.4391508
scal       7.8620111  9.6892411 11.5164712
male_diff -0.2963098 -0.2611253 -0.2259409
```

</details>

(We write `nlme::nlme()` and `nlme::intervals()`, naming the package each time, rather than loading nlme with `library()`. Loading it would hide some lme4 functions used in Section 13 behind nlme versions with the same name.)

Logs are hard to talk about, so turn the parameters into biological quantities:

```{r gc-summary}
gc_ci <- nlme::intervals(fit_gc, which = "fixed")$fixed   # columns lower, est., upper

tibble(
  quantity = c("Final length, females (mm)",
               "Final length, males / females",
               "Day of fastest relative growth (dpi)",
               "Peak growth rate (% longer per day)"),
  estimate = c(exp(gc_ci["hi", "est."]) / 1000,
               exp(gc_ci["male_diff", "est."]),
               gc_ci["xmid", "est."],
               100 * (gc_ci["hi", "est."] - gc_ci["lo", "est."]) / (4 * gc_ci["scal", "est."])),
  lower    = c(exp(gc_ci["hi", "lower"]) / 1000, exp(gc_ci["male_diff", "lower"]), gc_ci["xmid", "lower"], NA),
  upper    = c(exp(gc_ci["hi", "upper"]) / 1000, exp(gc_ci["male_diff", "upper"]), gc_ci["xmid", "upper"], NA)
)
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  quantity                             estimate  lower  upper
  <chr>                                   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Final length, females (mm)             45.1   35.4   57.5  
2 Final length, males / females           0.770  0.744  0.798
3 Day of fastest relative growth (dpi)   14.5   12.6   16.4  
4 Peak growth rate (% longer per day)    17.1   NA     NA    
```

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- **Final length.** Females level off at about **45 mm** (95% CI 35 to 58 mm). The interval is wide, and the whole estimate lies beyond the data (Section 14.5).
- **Sex.** Males level off at **0.77** of the female length, about 23% shorter (CI 20 to 26%). That agrees with Section 13.3, where females were about 27% longer than males (1 ÷ 1.27 = 0.79).
- **Fastest relative growth** is at about **14.5 dpi** (CI 12.6 to 16.4), around the L3 stage, when the worms get about **17% longer every day**.
- The peak growth rate has no confidence interval here, because it combines three parameters (`hi`, `lo` and `scal`). Getting one needs more advanced methods, such as bootstrapping.
- Compare with `nls()` (Section 14.2): the estimates moved a little once the mouse was included, and the intervals now reflect the number of mice, as in Section 13.
:::

### 14.4 Plot the curve

Predict the curve on a fine grid of days, for females and males, then draw it over the data. Panel B shows the **growth rate**: how much the log length changes from one day to the next, times 100, which is roughly "% longer per day". We draw the curves to 60 dpi on purpose, to show what the model claims beyond the data.

```{r fig-growthcurve, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
gc_est <- nlme::fixef(fit_gc)   # the fitted parameters: lo, hi, xmid, scal, male_diff

gc_pred <- expand_grid(dpi = seq(0, 60, by = 0.1), sex = c("Female", "Male")) |>
  mutate(male    = as.numeric(sex == "Male"),
         log_len = growth_curve(dpi, gc_est["lo"], gc_est["hi"] + gc_est["male_diff"] * male,
                                gc_est["xmid"], gc_est["scal"])) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  mutate(rate = 100 * (log_len - lag(log_len)) / 0.1) |>   # change in log length per day, as %
  ungroup() |>
  filter(sex == "Female" | dpi >= 21)    # sexes can't be told apart before L4 (21 dpi)

# grey band: days after the last sampling day
beyond_data <- annotate("rect", xmin = 42, xmax = 60, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90")

p_gc1 <- ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 42, xmax = 60, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +   # 0 is -Inf on a log axis
  geom_point(data = gc_data, aes(dpi, wb_length / 1000, colour = coalesce(as.character(sex), "Larva")),
             alpha = 0.5, position = position_jitter(width = 0.8, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_line(data = gc_pred, aes(dpi, exp(log_len) / 1000, linetype = sex), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Larva = "grey50", Female = "#E6AB02", Male = "#A6761D"),
                      breaks = c("Larva", "Female", "Male")) +
  labs(x = "Days post infection (dpi)", y = "Whole-body length (mm, log scale)",
       colour = "Worms", linetype = "Curve", title = "A. Fitted growth curve")

p_gc2 <- ggplot(filter(gc_pred, !is.na(rate)), aes(dpi, rate, linetype = sex)) +
  beyond_data +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = gc_est["xmid"], linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Days post infection (dpi)", y = "Growth rate (% longer per day)",
       linetype = "Curve", title = "B. Growth rate") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_gc1 + p_gc2 + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 2))
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your figure: click to see what it should look like</summary>

![Expected result. The same image is in the project folder as `expected_figures/fig-growthcurve.png`.](expected_figures/fig-growthcurve.png)

</details>

::: {.callout .callout-read}
::: {.callout-title}
How to read this
:::

- **Panel A.** The solid line is the female curve, and the dashed line the male curve. The male curve is drawn from 21 dpi (L4), the first stage that can be sexed. The sex difference was estimated from the adults only.
- The curve runs through the middle of most groups. Section 14.5 checks how closely.
- **The grey zone** is beyond the last sampling day. The curve keeps rising towards its plateau there, but no worm was measured.
- **Panel B.** The growth rate peaks at about 17% per day around 14 to 15 dpi (dotted line), then falls. By 42 dpi the worms are still growing about 3 to 4% per day, which is why the plateau lies beyond the data.
- This is the **relative** growth rate (% per day). In mm per day, growth peaks later, because a 4% increase in a 25 mm adult is far more length than 17% of a 1 mm larva.
:::

### 14.5 Check the fit, and know its limits

Residuals are how far each worm sits from the curve (on the log scale, so 0.1 is about 10%). Average them by group: if the curve fits, each group's average should be near 0.

```{r gc-resid}
gc_data |>
  mutate(resid = resid(fit_gc, level = 0)) |>   # level = 0: the population curve, without mouse shifts
  group_by(dpi, lifestage) |>
  summarise(n_worms = n(), mean_resid = round(mean(resid), 3), .groups = "drop")
```

<details class="expected-figure">
<summary>Check your output: click to see what it should look like</summary>

```
# A tibble: 8 × 4
    dpi lifestage    n_worms mean_resid
  <dbl> <fct>          <int>      <dbl>
1     3 L1                20     -0.021
2     9 L2                20      0.05 
3    14 L3                25      0.027
4    21 L4                25     -0.09 
5    35 Adult female      30      0.11 
6    35 Adult male        30      0.098
7    42 Adult female      25     -0.089
8    42 Adult male        25     -0.083
```

</details>

The averages are all within about ±0.1 (10%), but they are **not random**. L4 at 21 dpi sits about 9% below the curve, the adults at 35 dpi about 10% above it, and the adults at 42 dpi about 9% below it. A pattern like this, rather than scattered noise, means the curve's shape doesn't quite match the data:

- The jump from L4 to adult is bigger than a smooth curve allows (limit 3 below).
- From 35 to 42 dpi the worms grow less than the curve predicts. Growth may be slowing faster than the logistic shape assumes, so the real final size may be **smaller** than 45 mm.

None of this makes the curve useless: it is still a fair summary of the overall trend. But it is a reason to report the plateau cautiously.

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
::: {.callout-title}
Four limits to keep in mind
:::

1. **The final size is an extrapolation.** The last sampling day is 42 dpi, where females average about 29 mm. The plateau of about 45 mm comes from the *shape* of the curve, not from worms anyone measured. Its confidence interval assumes the logistic shape is right. To pin it down you need later timepoints (Exercise 7 shows how much it depends on the last one).
2. **Few timepoints.** Here 6 sampling days support 5 parameters. That works, but there's no room for anything more complex, such as a separate curve shape for each sex.
3. **Nematodes grow in steps.** Growth happens mainly between moults, so a smooth curve is a simplification. It describes the overall trend, not the moults.
4. **`lo` is not the size at hatching.** exp(4.09) is about 60 µm, smaller than any worm: it is where the curve would level off long before hatching. To get the size at hatching, ask the curve for its prediction at 0 dpi: `exp(growth_curve(0, gc_est["lo"], gc_est["hi"], gc_est["xmid"], gc_est["scal"]))` gives about 200 µm. The newly hatched larvae, which weren't used in the fit, measure about 225 µm, so this is a fair check, and the curve passes it reasonably well.

The alternative is a smooth curve with no fixed shape (a GAM, `mgcv::gam(log(wb_length) ~ s(dpi, k = 5) + s(host_id, bs = "re"))`, with `host_id` as a factor). It is easier to fit and assumes less, but it has no parameters to interpret and can't say anything beyond the last timepoint. It is a good check on the logistic curve.
:::

## 16. Practice exercises

Try each exercise yourself first. Open the green **Hint** box only if you are stuck. Write your answers in new chunks: put the cursor on an empty line and press `Ctrl + Alt + I` (`Cmd + Option + I` on a Mac) to insert one.

**1. Fill in the template.** Enter 10 to 15 of your own worms in `trichuris_morphometrics_data_template.xlsx`, export the `data` sheet as CSV (UTF-8), and read it in Section 3.4. Which drop-down or number check caught a mistake as you typed?

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

In Excel: *File > Save As*, then choose **CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited)**. Save the file in the `data` folder, then read it with `read_csv("data/your_file.csv")`. Run `glimpse()` on the result: every measurement column should say `<dbl>` (a number). A `<chr>` (text) there means a cell in that column contains text.

</details>

**2. Break the data on purpose.** Make a copy of the messy CSV (for example `data/my_messy_copy.csv`) and work on the copy. Change one label to "Adult - female" (a hyphen instead of the en dash). Then change one length in the `WB Length` column to "250 um" (units in the cell). Read the copy in Section 3.1 instead of the original, and rerun 3.1 and 3.2. What changes?

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

- **The hyphen.** The `count(Lifestage)` table in Section 3.2 now has **9 rows instead of 8**: "Adult - female" shows up as its own group of 1, and "Adult – Female" drops to 54. To R they are different labels. Without the count table you would never notice.
- **"250 um".** In `glimpse()`, `WB Length` is now `<chr>` (text) instead of `<dbl>`: `read_csv()` reads the **whole column as text**, not just that one cell. Any arithmetic on it, such as `` messy$`WB Length` / 1000 ``, stops with `non-numeric argument to binary operator`.

</details>

**3. Mouse effect on composition.** Model `st_pct` with a mouse random effect: `lmer(st_pct ~ lifestage + (1 | host_id), data = filter(worms, !is.na(host_id)))`. What is the ICC? Does the stichosome share vary more between mice than the length does?

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

Store the model, then reuse the ICC code from Section 13.4:

```r
fit_st_pct <- lmer(st_pct ~ lifestage + (1 | host_id), data = filter(worms, !is.na(host_id)))
VarCorr(fit_st_pct) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(icc = round(vcov[grp == "host_id"] / sum(vcov), 2))
```

You should get an ICC of about **0.47**, compared with **0.43** for adult length in Section 13.4. So the stichosome share is at least as strongly clustered by mouse as length is.

</details>

**4. PC scores.** Model shape PC1 (Section 10.1) against lifestage with a mouse random effect. Which stage differences remain clear once mouse is accounted for?

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

```r
fit_pc1 <- lmer(PC1 ~ lifestage + (1 | host_id), data = filter(shape_scores, !is.na(host_id)))
emmeans(fit_pc1, pairwise ~ lifestage, lmer.df = "satterthwaite")
```

The second half of the output (`$contrasts`) compares every pair of lifestages, with p-values adjusted for making many comparisons.

</details>

**5. Within-stage allometry.** Repeat the stichosome scaling slope (Section 13.7) for adults only. Does it differ from the pooled slope?

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

Filter `seg_long` to adults before fitting:

```r
st_adults <- seg_long |> filter(segment == "Stichosome", !is.na(host_id), stage == "Adult")
fit_st_adults <- lmer(log10(length_um) ~ log10(wb_length) + (1 | host_id), data = st_adults)
slope_row(fit_st_adults, "lmer, adults only")
```

You should get a slope of about **0.98** (95% CI about 0.88 to 1.08), from 41 worms. That is close to isometry (1), and lower than the pooled 1.08. Within adults the stichosome keeps its share: the pooled slope mostly reflects the change *between* stages.

</details>

**6. (Advanced, optional) Power and mice.** This one needs you to edit a long chunk of code. Edit the R simulation chunk in Appendix C (set `eval = TRUE` in the chunk header, or just run it with its ▶ button) to use 8 mice per timepoint instead of 4 or 5, with the same number of worms in total. The chunk writes your simulated worms twice: as a messy sheet and in the tidy layout. Point Section 3.4 at `data/my_simulation_tidy.csv` instead of the provided tidy file. Rerun Section 13.6: how do the mixed-model intervals change? Then try 3 mice with twice as many worms each. (Your numbers will differ from the provided files, because the random numbers differ.)

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

The number of mice per timepoint is set in one line of the simulation chunk, the one starting `n_mice = c(4, 4,`. Change the six numbers to `8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8`. In Section 3.4, change the file name to `data/my_simulation_tidy.csv`. Expect the red (mixed-model) intervals in Section 13.6 to get narrower with more mice, even though the number of worms is unchanged.

</details>

**7. How much does the final size depend on the last timepoint?** Refit the growth curve from Section 14.3 without the 42 dpi worms. How does the estimated final length of females change?

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

Filter the data, then reuse the model code with the new data:

```r
gc_no42 <- filter(gc_data, dpi < 42)

fit_gc_no42 <- nlme::nlme(log(wb_length) ~ growth_curve(dpi, lo, hi + male_diff * male, xmid, scal) + mouse,
                          data   = gc_no42,
                          fixed  = lo + hi + xmid + scal + male_diff ~ 1,
                          random = mouse ~ 1 | host_id,
                          start  = coef(fit_gc_nls))

exp(nlme::intervals(fit_gc_no42, which = "fixed")$fixed["hi", ]) / 1000   # final length (mm)
```

Without the 42 dpi worms, the estimated female final length jumps to about **236 mm** (95% CI 44 to 1,260 mm), against 45 mm with them. Up to 35 dpi the data show hardly any slowing down, so the curve has almost nothing to tell it where the plateau is, and the estimate becomes meaningless. A growth curve's final size is only as good as your latest timepoints: if final size matters, keep sampling until growth has clearly stopped.

</details>

**8. A log-ratio for one pair of regions.** In Section 7.2, every centred log-ratio shifts a little when some regions change a lot between the sexes. When the question is about one pair of regions, a simple log-ratio avoids that. Is the intestine longer relative to the stichosome in males than in females? Model `log(intestine / st)` against `sex` in adults.

<details class="hint">
<summary>Hint</summary>

```r
adults_ratio <- worms |> filter(stage == "Adult", !is.na(st), !is.na(intestine))
fit_ratio <- lm(log(intestine / st) ~ sex, data = adults_ratio)
exp(cbind(estimate = coef(fit_ratio), confint(fit_ratio)))["sexMale", ]
```

You should get about **1.03** (95% CI 0.94 to 1.13, p = 0.51), from 41 worms: relative to the stichosome, the male intestine is about 3% longer, and the interval includes no difference.

The simulation built in a true difference of about 6% (intestine 19% against 18% of the body, stichosome 52% in both, Appendix C). That is too small to detect reliably with 41 worms, especially as stichosome length also varies between mice, which makes it a noisy reference. The 8% difference from the centred log-ratio in Section 7.2 was partly this real difference and partly the shift in the worm's average region. Every log-ratio answers the question "relative to what?", so choose the one that matches your question.

</details>

**9. Your data.** Put your data in the template layout (Appendix B), point Section 3.4 at your CSV, and run Sections 3.4 to 15. Before that, try the checks from Section 3.1 to 3.3 on your original sheet: what problems do they turn up?

## 17. Where to go next

- **Random slopes.** If the effect of sex or timepoint differs between mice, use `(1 + sex | host_id)` (needs enough worms per mouse and enough mice).
- **More levels of grouping.** If mice come from several experiments, cages or batches, nest the random effects: `(1 | experiment/host_id)`, or `(1 | experiment) + (1 | host_id)` if mice appear in only one experiment.
- **Worms with no host.** For in vitro hatched larvae, a `batch` column (hatching date or egg batch) can play the role of `host_id`, so they can be included in the mixed models.
- **Mice sampled repeatedly.** If a mouse contributes worms at more than one timepoint, the dpi comparison becomes within-mouse, which changes the model and the power. Check Section 12.2 on your real data.
- **Other growth curves.** Section 14 used a logistic curve. Gompertz and von Bertalanffy curves have different shapes and are worth comparing (`AIC()` helps choose between models fitted to the same data). A smooth curve with no fixed shape (`mgcv::gam`, with `s(host_id, bs = "re")` for mouse) is a useful check.
- **More compositional methods.** The `compositions` package has isometric log-ratios (for models with several regions at once) and ways to handle regions that are zero or missing, such as the ovary/testis in young larvae.
- **Very few mice.** Bayesian models (`brms`) handle small numbers of mice more transparently than classical mixed models.
- **True geometric morphometrics.** If you digitise landmark coordinates from images, the `geomorph` package (Procrustes superimposition, then PCA on shape) is the standard route.
- **Classifying groups.** If you want to ask how well measurements discriminate lifestages or species, look at `MASS::lda()` or the `MorphoTools2` package.

## Appendix A: R in ten minutes

You only need a few ideas to follow the code. Run each chunk below, in order, and look at what it prints. These chunks don't need anything from the main tutorial, so you can run them before Section 0. (Lines starting with `#` are **comments**: notes for humans, which R ignores.)

**Objects and `<-`.** `<-` stores a value under a name, so you can use it later. Read it as "gets".

```{r r-basics-objects}
n_worms <- 230        # n_worms "gets" 230
n_worms * 2           # use it: R prints the answer below the chunk
```

**Vectors with `c()`.** `c()` combines several values into one **vector**. Most R operations work on every element at once.

```{r r-basics-vectors}
lengths_um <- c(218.2, 205.5, 235.5)
lengths_um / 1000          # every value converted to mm
mean(lengths_um)           # mean() is a function; lengths_um is its argument
```

**Functions and arguments.** A function does a job: `mean(x)`, `round(x, digits = 1)`. The values inside the brackets are its **arguments**. Named arguments like `digits = 1` change how it behaves. For help on any function, run `?round` in the Console.

**Missing values: `NA`.** R writes a blank cell as `NA` ("not available"). Most calculations give `NA` if any value is missing, unless you say to skip them with `na.rm = TRUE`.

```{r r-basics-na}
x <- c(10, NA, 30)
mean(x)                    # NA: R won't guess the missing value
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)      # 20: ignore the missing value
is.na(x)                   # TRUE where a value is missing
```

**Data frames (tibbles).** A spreadsheet-like table is a **data frame**. The tidyverse version is called a **tibble**. Each column is a vector. `toy$length` or `toy |> pull(length)` picks one column out. You will see both styles.

```{r r-basics-tibble}
library(tidyverse)
toy <- tibble(sample = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
              stage  = c("L1", "L1", "Adult"),
              length = c(220, 240, 25000))
toy
toy$length               # base R way to pick one column
toy |> pull(length)      # tidyverse way: the same values
```

**Factors.** A **factor** is a categorical variable with a fixed set of **levels** in a set order. Plots and models use that order, so we set it ourselves rather than accept the alphabetical one.

```{r r-basics-factor}
factor(c("L2", "Adult", "L1"), levels = c("L1", "L2", "Adult"))
```

**The pipe `|>`.** Read `|>` as "**and then**". It passes the result on the left into the function on the right, so a long job reads top to bottom:

```{r r-basics-pipe}
toy |>
  filter(stage == "L1") |>          # keep L1 rows  (== means "is equal to")
  summarise(mean_length = mean(length))
```

You will often see **`%>%`** in other tutorials, online answers and older scripts. It is the tidyverse's original pipe, and for everything in this tutorial it does the same job as `|>`. `toy %>% filter(stage == "L1")` and `toy |> filter(stage == "L1")` give the same result. This tutorial uses `|>` because it is built into R (version 4.1 or newer) and is what the tidyverse now recommends.

**Small functions written in place: `\(x)`.** You will often see code such as `\(x) x / 1000`. This is a short **function without a name**: "take a value, call it `x`, and return `x / 1000`". It is used with helpers like `across()`, which apply the same job to several columns:

```{r r-basics-lambda}
convert_to_mm <- \(x) x / 1000     # a function stored under a name...
convert_to_mm(25000)

toy |> mutate(across(c(length), \(x) x / 1000))   # ...or used in place, unnamed
```

**Packages.** Extra tools come in **packages**. `install.packages("name")` downloads one **once per computer**. `library(name)` switches it on **in every new session**.

## Appendix B: how to set out your own data table

Read this before you collect or enter your own measurements. The most important step happens **before you open R**: how the spreadsheet is laid out. A well-laid-out table makes the analysis easy, and a badly laid-out one means hours of cleaning. The rule is **tidy data**:

> **One row per worm. One column per variable. One value per cell.**

### Two starting points

1. **You are about to enter new data.** Use the template workbook that comes with this tutorial, `trichuris_morphometrics_data_template.xlsx`. It has a `data` sheet with the columns below, drop-down lists for `lifestage`, `sex` and `source`, number checks on the measurement columns, a `data_dictionary` sheet, an `example` sheet of six worms, and a `README` sheet. Export the `data` sheet as CSV (UTF-8) and go to Section 3.4.
2. **You already have a spreadsheet.** Rebuild it once in the template layout (the tips at the end of this appendix help), rather than writing code to convert it. Section 3 shows the kinds of problem to look for in the original.

### Recommended columns

Dark-blue headers in the template are the core columns, and lighter ones are optional.

| Column | What goes in it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `sample` | Unique ID, one per worm | S001 |
| `host_id` | The mouse the worm came from (blank if it did not come from a host) | M07 |
| `batch` | Optional: experiment, infection cohort, hatching batch or cage | EXP2 |
| `dpi` | Days post infection (a number only) | 21 |
| `lifestage` | L1, L2, L3, L4 or Adult | Adult |
| `sex` | Female, Male, or blank if not sexed | Female |
| `source` | Where the worm came from: `host` or `hatched in vitro` | host |
| `wb_length_um`, `ant_nr_um`, `nr_st_um`, `st_um`, ... | One column per raw measurement, in µm, **numbers only** | 24980 |
| `st_number` | Approximate stichosome number | 55 |
| `observer`, `measured_on` | Optional: who measured it and when (useful for checking measurement drift) | AB, 2026-03-14 |
| `notes` | Free text for anything unusual | tail broken |

Note that **stage and sex are separate columns**. Putting both in one cell (for example "Adult – Female") forces you to split them apart before every analysis, and it makes it impossible to ask a question such as "does sex matter across all adult timepoints?" without cleaning first.


### How to spot a column that needs splitting

Look for these signs in a column:

- **A separator inside the values**: a dash, slash, semicolon, comma or brackets ("Adult – Female", "St (or end of Os)").
- **A qualifier tacked on**: "L1 – newly hatched" adds a note about origin to a stage.
- **A value plus a unit**: "250 µm" in a cell.
- **A range or approximation**: "40–45" or "~40" in a count cell.
- **A compound ID** that packs two things together, for example "M07-S12" for host and worm.
- **A question you can't answer with a simple filter**: if "all adults, regardless of sex" needs text matching, the column holds two variables.

**Split a column when each part is something you might filter, group or plot by on its own.** Don't split an ID such as "S001" that you would never analyse in pieces.

Three questions to ask about every column:

1. **Does it hold one variable only?** "Adult – Female" holds two (stage and sex). "L1 – newly hatched" holds two (stage and where the worm came from).
2. **Is every value spelled the same way?** "L1", "l1", "L1 " (trailing space) and "Larva 1" are four different categories to R. Use drop-down lists.
3. **Could it be calculated from other columns?** If so, don't type it. Percentages of total length can be computed in R from the lengths, so they never disagree with the lengths.

### Avoid and instead

| Avoid | Instead |
|---|---|
| "Adult – Female" (stage and sex in one cell) | `lifestage` = "Adult", `sex` = "Female" |
| "L1 – newly hatched" mixed in with "L1" in the same column | `lifestage` = "L1" for both, and record the difference in `source` (or with `dpi` = 0) |
| Typing the same category differently ("L1", "l1", "L1 ", "Larva 1") | One spelling, always. Use a drop-down list in your spreadsheet to enforce it |
| Long headers with spaces, line breaks and symbols ("% of Total – NR to Entrance of St (or end of Os)") | Short plain headers with units: `nr_st_um`. Put the full description in the data dictionary |
| Units inside cells ("250 µm") | Units in the header only. A cell with "250 µm" is read as text, not a number |
| Zero for "not measured", or "-", "n/a", "?" | Leave the cell blank. Use 0 only when the measurement really was zero |
| Percent-of-total columns calculated in the spreadsheet | Record raw lengths only and let R calculate percentages. This avoids copy/paste and arithmetic errors |
| Merged cells, blank rows, blank columns, totals or averages under the data | One header row, then data only, with no gaps |
| Colours or bold text carrying information (for example red = damaged) | A real column such as `notes` or `damaged` (yes/no). Colours are lost when you export |
| Dates as "3/4/26" (ambiguous) | ISO format: 2026-04-03 |
| Recording a sum and all its parts without checking they agree | If you record `ant_nr_um`, `nr_st_um` **and** `ant_st_um`, check that the first two add up to the third (Section 5.2) |

### Suggested splits for a typical lab sheet (like the practice file)

| Current column | Suggestion |
|---|---|
| `Lifestage` ("L1 – newly hatched", "Adult – Female") | Three columns: `lifestage` (L1 to L4, Adult), `sex` (Female, Male, blank if not sexed) and `source` (host, hatched in vitro) |
| `Timepoint (dpi)` | Keep as a number. Use 0 for larvae hatched in vitro |
| `Sample` | Keep as a unique worm ID. Add `host_id` for the mouse, and `batch` if worms came from different experiments or hatching batches |
| `Anterior body end to Entrance of St (or end of Os)` | The "(or end of Os)" suggests two landmarks share one column. If the stichosome entrance and the end of the oesophagus are the same point in some stages but not others, record one landmark consistently, or add a column saying which one was measured |
| `Ov/Ts` and `Rt/Cl` | Keep each as a single length column. `sex` already says whether it is ovary or testis, rectum or cloaca |
| `Rest of body` | If you work it out by subtraction (whole body minus the other regions), you don't need to type it: it can be calculated. Keep the column only if you measured it directly |
| `% of Total – ...` columns | Don't record these. R calculates them from the lengths |
| `APPROX. St numbers` | If it contains ranges ("40–45") or symbols ("~40"), keep the column numeric: record one best estimate and put the uncertainty in `notes`, or use separate minimum and maximum columns |

### When to combine instead

The opposite problem is **one variable spread across several columns**, for example separate "Female length" and "Male length" columns, or one column per timepoint. Those should be a single `length` column plus `sex` or `dpi`.

The design used here (one row per worm, one column per landmark) is already the right shape. Move to **one row per measurement** only if the same worm is measured more than once, for example by several observers. In that case add `observer` and `replicate` columns.

### The data dictionary

A data dictionary is a table that says what every column means. It is the most useful thing you can give a collaborator (or yourself in a year). The template contains a full one. Here is the shape of it:

| column | meaning | type | unit | allowed values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sample` | Unique ID for each worm | text | | never repeated |
| `dpi` | Days post infection (0 = hatched in vitro) | whole number | days | 0 or more |
| `lifestage` | Developmental stage | list | | L1, L2, L3, L4, Adult |
| `sex` | Sex; blank if not sexed | list | | Female, Male |
| `wb_length_um` | Whole-body length | number | µm | 0 or more |

It should also say what a **blank** means. For example: "blank in `ov_ts_um` means the organ was not yet present (early larvae) or not measured. It does *not* mean zero."

### General habits for tidy data

**Column names**

- Short, lowercase, with underscores and no spaces or symbols.
- Put the unit in the name (`wb_length_um`) and keep a consistent order (`ant_nr` before `nr_st`).
- Never start a name with a digit.

**Categories**

- One fixed spelling for each category, enforced with a drop-down list.
- Watch for trailing spaces, capitalisation differences and en dashes versus hyphens. Each creates a new group in R.
- Put explanations in a `notes` column, never inside the category.

**Missing values**

- Leave cells blank. Don't use 0, "-", "n/a" or "?".
- A blank can mean "not measured" or "not applicable" (an ovary in an early larva). Say what it means in the data dictionary. If R needs to tell the two apart, add a column that records it.

**IDs and structure**

- Keep IDs unique and spelled identically every time ("M07", never "M7").
- Record every grouping factor that might make worms resemble each other: host, batch, observer, measurement date.

**Sheet hygiene**

- One table per sheet and one header row.
- No merged cells, blank rows, subtotals, or colour used as data.
- ISO dates (2026-04-03).

**Raw versus calculated**

- Record only what you measured. Percentages, totals and differences can be calculated.
- If you do record a sum and all its parts, check they agree (Section 5.2).

**Documentation and checks**

- Write a data dictionary: meaning, unit, allowed values, and what a blank means.
- Keep the raw file untouched.
- Run the same checks every time you add data: unique IDs, plausible ranges, parts that add up, and a count of rows per group.

### Making the rebuild easier

- Start from the template workbook so the headers, drop-downs and dictionary are already set up.
- Paste measurement columns in as **values only**, so spreadsheet formatting doesn't come along.
- Excel and Google Sheets can split "Adult – Female" with *Text to Columns*, using the delimiter " – " (a space, an en dash, a space). Then fill `source` with a filter.
- Enter new data straight into the tidy layout, so you won't need to convert it again.

## Appendix C: how the practice data were simulated

The practice files were made by `tools/make_simulated_data.py`. The R chunk below is the **same design written in R**: how many worms per timepoint, their average size and body proportions, the mouse effects, and the deliberate untidiness (spreadsheet headers, stray spaces, transcription errors and empty rows). Reading it shows exactly what structure the analyses are meant to recover, for example that mice differ in worm size, which is why the mixed models in Section 13 are needed.

It is **not run** when you knit (`eval = FALSE`), and you only need to run it for Exercise 6. If you do run it, it writes `data/my_simulation_messy.csv` and the same worms in the tidy layout, `data/my_simulation_tidy.csv`. Its random numbers differ from the provided files, so don't mix the two.

```{r simulate, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)

# Design: how many worms per timepoint / lifestage, and their average size (µm)
design <- tribble(
  ~dpi, ~lifestage,            ~mean_length_um, ~n,
  0,    "L1 (newly hatched)",        220,        30,
  3,    "L1",                        280,        20,
  9,    "L2",                        700,        20,
  14,   "L3",                       1500,        25,
  21,   "L4",                       4500,        25,
  35,   "Adult female",            25000,        30,
  35,   "Adult male",              20000,        30,
  42,   "Adult female",            28000,        25,
  42,   "Adult male",              22000,        25
)

# Average proportion of the body in each region, by lifestage (each row sums to 1)
prop_means <- tribble(
  ~lifestage,            ~p_ant_nr, ~p_nr_st, ~p_st, ~p_int, ~p_ov_ts, ~p_rt_cl, ~p_rest,
  "L1 (newly hatched)",    0.10,      0.08,    0.38,   0.30,   0.00,     0.04,     0.10,
  "L1",                    0.10,      0.08,    0.38,   0.30,   0.00,     0.04,     0.10,
  "L2",                    0.09,      0.08,    0.40,   0.28,   0.00,     0.04,     0.11,
  "L3",                    0.08,      0.07,    0.44,   0.25,   0.02,     0.03,     0.11,
  "L4",                    0.06,      0.06,    0.48,   0.22,   0.05,     0.03,     0.10,
  "Adult female",          0.04,      0.04,    0.52,   0.18,   0.12,     0.02,     0.08,
  "Adult male",            0.04,      0.04,    0.52,   0.19,   0.06,     0.02,     0.13
)

# Mice: each mouse is culled at ONE timepoint, so mice are nested within dpi.
# Each mouse gets its own random shift in worm size and in relative stichosome length.
mice <- tibble(dpi    = c(3, 9, 14, 21, 35, 42),
               n_mice = c(4, 4,  5,  5,  5,  5)) |>
  uncount(n_mice) |>
  mutate(
    host_id         = sprintf("M%02d", row_number()),
    mouse_size      = rnorm(n(), 0, 0.08),
    mouse_st_effect = rnorm(n(), 0, 0.06)
  )

# The mice available at each timepoint (none at dpi 0: those larvae were hatched in vitro)
host_pool <- mice |>
  group_by(dpi) |>
  summarise(hosts = list(host_id), .groups = "drop")

sim <- design |>
  left_join(prop_means, by = "lifestage") |>
  uncount(n) |>                                    # one row per worm
  left_join(host_pool, by = "dpi") |>
  mutate(host_id = map_chr(hosts, \(h) if (is.null(h)) NA_character_ else base::sample(h, 1))) |>
  select(-hosts) |>
  left_join(select(mice, host_id, mouse_size, mouse_st_effect), by = "host_id") |>
  mutate(
    sample = sprintf("S%03d", row_number()),

    # worms with no host get no mouse effect
    across(c(mouse_size, mouse_st_effect), \(x) replace_na(x, 0)),

    # worm size: lifestage average x mouse effect x individual variation
    wb_length = mean_length_um * exp(mouse_size + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.08)),

    # relative stichosome length also varies by mouse
    p_st = p_st * exp(mouse_st_effect),

    # add individual variation to each proportion, then rescale to sum to 1
    across(starts_with("p_"), \(p) p * exp(rnorm(length(p), 0, 0.08))),
    total_p = p_ant_nr + p_nr_st + p_st + p_int + p_ov_ts + p_rt_cl + p_rest,
    across(starts_with("p_"), \(p) p / total_p),

    # absolute lengths (µm)
    ant_nr    = p_ant_nr * wb_length,
    nr_st     = p_nr_st  * wb_length,
    ant_st    = ant_nr + nr_st,
    st        = p_st     * wb_length,
    intestine = p_int    * wb_length,
    ov_ts     = p_ov_ts  * wb_length,
    rt_cl     = p_rt_cl  * wb_length,
    rest      = p_rest   * wb_length,

    # percentages of whole-body length
    ant_nr_pct    = p_ant_nr * 100,
    nr_st_pct     = p_nr_st  * 100,
    ant_st_pct    = ant_st / wb_length * 100,
    st_pct        = p_st     * 100,
    intestine_pct = p_int    * 100,
    ov_ts_pct     = p_ov_ts  * 100,
    rt_cl_pct     = p_rt_cl  * 100,
    rest_pct      = p_rest   * 100,

    # approximate stichosome number: fixed early in development (about 50 to 60), whatever the body size
    st_number = round(55 + rnorm(n(), 0, 2.5)),

    # which measurements did this worm get? (partial measurement)
    meas_set = base::sample(c("length_only", "head", "full"), n(),
                            replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.35, 0.25, 0.40)),
    st_number = if_else(meas_set == "full" &
                          !lifestage %in% c("L1 (newly hatched)", "L1") &
                          runif(n()) < 0.6,
                        st_number, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # head landmarks missing if the worm was only measured for length
    across(c(ant_nr, nr_st, ant_st, ant_nr_pct, nr_st_pct, ant_st_pct),
           \(x) if_else(meas_set == "length_only", NA_real_, x)),
    # body regions only present for fully measured worms
    across(c(st, intestine, ov_ts, rt_cl, rest,
             st_pct, intestine_pct, ov_ts_pct, rt_cl_pct, rest_pct),
           \(x) if_else(meas_set != "full", NA_real_, x)),
    # ovary/testis structurally absent in the youngest larvae
    across(c(ov_ts, ov_ts_pct),
           \(x) if_else(lifestage %in% c("L1 (newly hatched)", "L1", "L2"), NA_real_, x)),
    # round like a real spreadsheet
    across(c(wb_length, ant_nr, nr_st, ant_st, st, intestine, ov_ts, rt_cl, rest),
           \(x) round(x, 1)),
    across(ends_with("_pct"), \(x) round(x, 2)),

    # the lifestage label as it appears in the spreadsheet (stage and sex combined)
    lifestage_raw = recode(lifestage,
                           "L1 (newly hatched)" = "L1 \u2013 newly hatched",
                           "Adult female"       = "Adult \u2013 Female",
                           "Adult male"         = "Adult \u2013 Male",
                           .default = lifestage)
  )

# Slip in two transcription errors (ant_st inflated) for the QC step to find
sim <- sim |>
  mutate(ant_st_n = cumsum(!is.na(ant_st)),        # 1, 2, 3 ... counting only worms with ant_st
         ant_st   = if_else(!is.na(ant_st) & ant_st_n %in% c(7, 53), ant_st * 1.6, ant_st)) |>
  select(-ant_st_n)

# Spreadsheet-style headers (what the real file looks like)
raw_headers <- c(
  "Timepoint (dpi)", "Lifestage", "Sample", "Host ID", "WB Length",
  "Anterior body end to NR",
  "% of Total \u2013 Anterior body end to NR",
  "Anterior body end to Entrance of St (or end of Os)",
  "% of Total \u2013 Anterior body end to Entrance of St (or end of Os)",
  "NR to Entrance of St (or end of Os)",
  "% of Total \u2013 NR to Entrance of St (or end of Os)",
  "St", "% of Total \u2013 St",
  "Int", "% of Total \u2013 Int",
  "Ov/Ts", "% of Total \u2013 Ov/Ts",
  "Rt/Cl", "% of Total \u2013 Rt/Cl",
  "Rest of body", "% of Total \u2013 Rest of body",
  "APPROX. St numbers"
)

worms_raw_sim <- sim |>
  select(dpi, lifestage_raw, sample, host_id, wb_length,
         ant_nr, ant_nr_pct, ant_st, ant_st_pct, nr_st, nr_st_pct,
         st, st_pct, intestine, intestine_pct, ov_ts, ov_ts_pct,
         rt_cl, rt_cl_pct, rest, rest_pct, st_number) |>
  set_names(raw_headers)

# Two stray trailing spaces in the lifestage labels (a very common typo)
worms_raw_sim <- worms_raw_sim |>
  mutate(Lifestage = if_else(row_number() %in% c(60, 140), str_c(Lifestage, " "), Lifestage))

# Eight completely empty rows at the bottom, as often left behind in a spreadsheet
worms_raw_sim <- bind_rows(worms_raw_sim, tibble(.rows = 8))

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(worms_raw_sim, "data/my_simulation_messy.csv", na = "")   # blank cells, like Excel

# The same worms in the tidy template layout, ready for Section 3.4 (Exercise 6)
sim_tidy <- sim |>
  mutate(sex       = case_when(lifestage == "Adult female" ~ "Female",
                               lifestage == "Adult male"   ~ "Male"),
         source    = if_else(lifestage == "L1 (newly hatched)", "hatched in vitro", "host"),
         lifestage = str_remove(lifestage, " .*")) |>     # "Adult female" -> "Adult", "L1 (newly hatched)" -> "L1"
  select(sample, host_id, dpi, lifestage, sex, source,
         wb_length, ant_nr, ant_st, nr_st, st, intestine, ov_ts, rt_cl, rest, st_number) |>
  rename_with(\(x) str_c(x, "_um"), wb_length:rest)
write_csv(sim_tidy, "data/my_simulation_tidy.csv", na = "")
```
